pattern.ordering: One judgment (or related pair) per passage, with short verbatim extracts and the historical background; constitutional, criminal, evidence, arbitration, environmental, technology and service law

Correct answer carries 1 mark; each wrong answer carries -0.25.

Passages are original summaries for practice, current to mid-November 2026. Verify pending or evolving matters (interim orders, referred or reviewed rulings) and check each verbatim extract against the official judgment text before publishing hit-and-run status, the BNS s.152 challenge, the marital-rape challenge, review proceedings on the PMLA ruling, scope of BNSS s.479 for old cases) against current official sources.
Every explanation includes why the other options fail, the CLAT trap, and any language trick.

passages.title: Governors, Presidents and Bills: The 2025 Presidential Reference on Articles 200 and 201
passages.passage: On 8 April 2025, in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor, a two-judge Bench (J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan JJ.) read a three-month outer limit into Articles 200 and 201 and, invoking Article 142, treated ten bills as having received 'deemed assent'. The President then referred fourteen questions to the Supreme Court under Article 143(1). A five-judge Bench (CJI B.R. Gavai, Surya Kant, Vikram Nath, P.S. Narasimha and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ.) delivered its opinion on 20 November 2025. Article 200 lets a Governor assent to a bill, withhold assent, or reserve it for the President; the first proviso says that a bill other than a money bill may be returned for reconsideration 'as soon as possible'. That phrase descends from draft Article 175 in the Constituent Assembly, which never replaced it with a fixed period, and Article 201 prescribes none for the President. As reported, the Court said that “the President, too, cannot be bound by judicially prescribed timelines in the discharge of functions under Article 201.” It rejected 'deemed assent' on the reasoning that one constitutional authority cannot substitute the role and powers of another, and held that decisions under Articles 200 and 201 are not justiciable on their merits before a bill becomes law. On the Governor's immunity it observed that Article 361 “is an absolute bar on judicial review in relation to personally subjecting the Governor to judicial proceedings”, yet “the constitutional office of the Governor is subject to the jurisdiction of this Court”, so that limited judicial intervention remains possible against “prolonged, unexplained and indefinite inaction”. The Bench described its advisory role as not amounting to 'judicial adjudication'. The history matters: the Court has answered references since Re Delhi Laws Act (1951) and Re Berubari Union (1960); Shamsher Singh (1974) held that the Governor ordinarily acts on ministerial advice; Nabam Rebia (2016) confined the Governor's discretion. Whether an Article 143 opinion binds courts under Article 141, and thereby displaces the April ruling, remains debated (verify current status).
verbatim_extracts: the President, too, cannot be bound by judicially prescribed timelines in the discharge of functions under Article 201.
is an absolute bar on judicial review in relation to personally subjecting the Governor to judicial proceedings
the constitutional office of the Governor is subject to the jurisdiction of this Court
prolonged, unexplained and indefinite inaction

questions.question: On the passage, why was the device of 'deemed assent' rejected in the 2025 opinion?

options.A: Because one constitutional authority cannot substitute the role and powers of another, so a deemed outcome could not be created even through Article 142
options.B: Because Article 142 cannot be invoked in any proceeding that arises from an Article 143 reference
options.C: Because the first proviso to Article 200 already treats a bill as assented to once the Governor keeps it for six weeks
options.D: Because assent is a legislative function which Parliament alone may regulate by passing a law

questions.explanation: The Bench's reasoning was institutional: courts cannot supply a decision that the Constitution commits to the Governor or the President. The phrase 'deemed assent' therefore found no home even under Article 142.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C invents a six-week rule that Article 200 does not contain. Option D mislabels the nature of assent and gives Parliament a power the passage does not mention. Option B states a limit on Article 142 that the passage never attributes to the Court.
questions.clat_trap: Options that sound procedural (six weeks, a parliamentary law) distract from the principle that was actually stated, namely substitution of one constitutional authority for another.
questions.language_trick: 'substitute the role and powers of another' is the operative phrase; 'deemed' means attributing a result without any decision by the authority.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the opinion as described in the passage?

options.A: The President cannot be bound by judicially prescribed timelines in the discharge of functions under Article 201
options.B: Article 361 bars subjecting the Governor personally to judicial proceedings, but the office remains answerable to the Court in a limited way
options.C: Decisions under Articles 200 and 201 are not justiciable on their merits before a bill becomes law, even though prolonged inaction may be examined
options.D: The constitutional office of the Governor lies wholly outside the jurisdiction of this Court

questions.explanation: The passage records that 'the constitutional office of the Governor is subject to the jurisdiction of this Court', so the statement that it lies wholly outside is the inconsistent one.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option A each restate what the opinion held as reported, so none of them is the odd one out.
questions.clat_trap: A NOT stem inverts the usual task: the correct answer is the false statement, while three accurate statements sit beside it as decoys. Students who skim for 'true' options pick one of those.
questions.language_trick: 'wholly outside' is an absolute phrase that the quoted sentence contradicts directly.

questions.question: A Governor keeps a bill without any message or reasons for eighteen months, and the State approaches the Court. On the passage, the Court

options.A: may issue a limited direction to the Governor to act, since prolonged, unexplained and indefinite inaction can be examined despite Article 361, but it cannot fix a deadline or declare the bill assented to
options.B: may declare the bill to have been assented to after three months, in line with the April 2025 ruling on deemed assent
options.C: may examine the merits of the bill and strike it down before it is enacted, since delay shows a doubt about validity
options.D: must dismiss the petition because Article 361 bars any proceeding concerning the Governor's inaction

questions.explanation: The opinion leaves room for limited intervention against indefinite inaction but denies timelines, deemed assent and pre-enactment review of merits.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reads Article 361 as covering the office, which the passage says is not so. Option B revives deemed assent. Option C permits pre-enactment merits review, which was held unavailable.
questions.clat_trap: The facts tempt the student to choose either total immunity or the April ruling's remedy; the correct answer sits between them.
questions.language_trick: 'limited direction' and 'cannot fix a deadline' mark the middle position.

questions.question: The 8 April 2025 decision and the 20 November 2025 opinion differ chiefly on

options.A: whether Article 143 permits the President to seek the Court's opinion on constitutional questions of public importance
options.B: whether a Governor may return a bill for reconsideration under the first proviso to Article 200 at all
options.C: whether timelines and deemed assent may be read into Articles 200 and 201
options.D: whether the Governor acts on ministerial advice in the exercise of ordinary legislative functions

questions.explanation: The April ruling read timelines and deemed assent into the Articles; the Reference Bench declined to do so.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option D and Option A are matters on which the two pronouncements are not said to differ.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options are accurate propositions about the topic but do not answer the 'differ chiefly' question.
questions.language_trick: 'chiefly' asks for the main point of difference, not any point of contact.

questions.question: The phrase 'as soon as possible' in the first proviso to Article 200 is best understood, on the passage, as

options.A: a direction with no numerical limit, which the Constituent Assembly left to the Governor's good sense instead of a fixed period
options.B: a rule under which continued silence ripens into assent after a reasonable time, so that the Governor's inaction operates as an implied approval of the bill
options.C: a six-week limit adopted from earlier constitutional practice, which the Court enforced as a mandatory condition on every Governor in its 2025 pronouncements
options.D: a directory expression that the Court held to carry no constitutional meaning at all

questions.explanation: The passage says the phrase descends from draft Article 175 and was never replaced by a fixed period; no timeline can therefore be read into it judicially.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C invents a numerical limit. Option B revives deemed assent through the back door. Option D overstates by denying any meaning to the phrase.
questions.clat_trap: The plausible wrong answers each supply a number or a consequence that the text lacks.
questions.language_trick: 'directory' is a term of art meaning non-binding in consequence, which is not the same as meaningless.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Court's refusal to fix timelines for Governors means that a Governor may hold a bill indefinitely without any judicial recourse. Reason (R): The opinion permits limited judicial intervention against prolonged, unexplained and indefinite inaction.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false, because the opinion allows limited intervention for indefinite inaction; R states exactly that and is true.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A cannot be accepted because refusing a deadline is not the same as giving immunity to inaction.
questions.clat_trap: The Assertion borrows the first half of the holding (no timelines) and exaggerates it into a no-remedy rule.
questions.language_trick: 'indefinitely' and 'any judicial recourse' are absolute expressions.

passages.title: The Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025 and the Supreme Court's Interim Order
passages.passage: The Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025 altered the framework of the Waqf Act 1995, which itself had replaced the 1954 Act. Its challenge invoked Articles 14, 25 and 26. On 15 September 2025 a Bench of CJI B.R. Gavai and Augustine George Masih J. delivered an interim order. It declined to stay the Act as a whole, holding, as reported, that “there is always a presumption of constitutionality in favour of a statute” and that a law “could be stayed in its entirety only in rarest of rare cases”. The Bench did, however, stay certain provisions on a prima facie view. The requirement that a person must have practised Islam for five years before creating a waqf was stayed until the State Governments frame rules for verifying such practice, since without a mechanism it would operate arbitrarily. The provision allowing an officer above the rank of Collector to decide whether disputed property is government land was stayed, along with consequential powers over revenue records. The abolition of waqf by user was not stayed; the Bench regarded it as prospective in operation. Registration requirements were not found arbitrary. On composition, the Bench indicated that the Central Waqf Council should have no more than four non-Muslim members out of twenty-two and a State Waqf Board no more than three out of eleven, and that the Chief Executive Officer of a Board be a Muslim 'as far as possible'. The history behind the dispute is long: in the Shirur Mutt case (1954) the Court separated matters of religion from the secular administration of religious property, which the State may regulate under Article 25(2)(a) and Article 26(d); in Ismail Faruqui (1994) it held that a mosque is not essential to the practice of Islam. The final hearing is pending (verify current status).
verbatim_extracts: there is always a presumption of constitutionality in favour of a statute
could be stayed in its entirety only in rarest of rare cases

questions.question: Why did the Bench refuse to stay the Act in its entirety?

options.A: Article 26 gives the Union exclusive power to legislate on religious endowments and bars all challenges to such legislation by any religious denomination
options.B: The petitioners had accepted the constitutional validity of all provisions except those relating to registration, so the rest of the Act stood unchallenged
options.C: The Act had already been in force for a period of five years before the challenge reached the Court
options.D: A statute carries a presumption of constitutionality, and a stay of the whole law is warranted only in the rarest of rare cases

questions.explanation: The Bench relied on the settled presumption of constitutionality and treated stay of an entire law as exceptional, before staying specific provisions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C and Option B invent facts that the passage does not give. Option A overstates Article 26 and ignores the Articles on which the challenge was based.
questions.clat_trap: The stem asks for the Court's stated reason, and wrong options offer plausible procedural reasons that were never given.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which of the following provisions was stayed by the interim order?

options.A: The requirement that a person must have practised Islam for five years before creating a waqf, until State rules provide a verification mechanism
options.B: The abolition of waqf by user, together with its effect on waqfs already registered before the amendment
options.C: The inclusion of non-Muslim members in the Central Waqf Council and in State Waqf Boards in any number
options.D: The requirement that a copy of the waqf deed accompany the application for registration of a waqf

questions.explanation: The five-year practice condition was stayed pending State rules. The abolition of waqf by user and the registration requirement were not stayed, and non-Muslim membership was addressed through numerical caps.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B was not stayed and was treated as prospective. Option D was not found arbitrary. Option C was not stayed but limited by caps.
questions.clat_trap: Every wrong option is a real provision in the Act that was discussed, so recall of what was stayed and what was merely limited is the whole test.
questions.language_trick: 'in any number' in the wrong option contradicts the caps the Bench indicated.

questions.question: A State Waqf Board of eleven members includes four non-Muslim members. On the passage, this composition

options.A: is valid, because the limit of four applies to State boards and the limit of three applies only to the Central Waqf Council
options.B: exceeds the limit the Bench indicated, which permits no more than three non-Muslim members in a State board of eleven
options.C: is invalid, because the Bench held that no non-Muslim may sit on a State Waqf Board
options.D: is valid, because the Bench stayed every limit on non-Muslim membership in State boards pending final hearing of the petitions

questions.explanation: The passage gives a cap of three of eleven for a State board and four of twenty-two for the Central Council; four of eleven therefore exceeds the State cap.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D says the limits were stayed, which is not what the passage reports. Option A swaps the two figures. Option C imagines a total exclusion that the Bench did not order.
questions.clat_trap: Two similar numbers (three and four) are attached to two different bodies, and the wrong options exploit the confusion.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The interim order is best characterised as

options.A: a ruling that decides the matter finally on the footing that waqf by user is retrospective
options.B: a decision that the Act is valid but that Article 26 prevents all State regulation of waqfs
options.C: a final declaration that the provisions not stayed are constitutional beyond challenge
options.D: a prima facie view that leaves the final questions of validity open

questions.explanation: The passage records an interim order based on a prima facie view; the final hearing is pending.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C treats an interim order as final. Option B states a legal result contrary to the passage. Option A reverses the Bench's view of prospectivity.
questions.clat_trap: An 'interim' order is often mistaken for a ruling on merits, and the wrong options attribute finality to it.
questions.language_trick: 'prima facie' signals a provisional assessment.

questions.question: Which earlier decision is most closely associated, in the passage, with the idea that the State may regulate the secular side of religious property while a denomination manages its religious affairs?

options.A: Shirur Mutt (1954), which held that religious denominations are entirely free to administer their property as they choose, without any statute
options.B: The Shirur Mutt case (1954), which separated matters of religion from the secular administration of religious property and left the latter open to regulation by law
options.C: The Waqf Act 1954, which the Court treated as a model of the permissible limits on legislative interference
options.D: Ismail Faruqui (1994), which held that a mosque is an essential part of Islamic practice, so that its acquisition by the State is barred

questions.explanation: The passage ties Shirur Mutt to the religion versus secular administration distinction and to Articles 25(2)(a) and 26(d).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reverses the holding in Ismail Faruqui. Option A misdescribes Shirur Mutt by ignoring regulation. Option C treats a statute as a judicial authority.
questions.clat_trap: The same case name appears in a correct and a distorted version, so the whole sentence has to be read.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the interim order and select the correct combination.
I. The Bench stayed the Waqf (Amendment) Act 2025 in its entirety.
II. The abolition of waqf by user was not stayed, the Bench treating it as prospective.
III. The five-year practice requirement for creating a waqf was stayed until State rules provide a verification mechanism.
IV. The Bench indicated limits on the number of non-Muslim members in the Central Waqf Council and State Waqf Boards.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements II, III and IV match the passage. Statement I is false because the Bench declined a blanket stay.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Combination (I and II) and (II and III) leave out IV, and (I, III and IV) includes the false statement I.
questions.clat_trap: The false statement I is the most dramatic and is placed first to attract students who recall the headline of the Act's challenge.
questions.language_trick: 'in its entirety' is an absolute phrase contradicted by the quoted sentence.

passages.title: Tribunals, Re-enactment and the Limits of Legislative Override: Madras Bar Association (2025)
passages.passage: Tribunals entered the constitutional scheme through the Forty-second Amendment (1976), which inserted Articles 323A and 323B. In L. Chandra Kumar (1997) the Court held that tribunal decisions remain open to High Court scrutiny under Articles 226 and 227, treating judicial review as part of the basic structure. A series of Madras Bar Association cases followed; in 2021 the Court struck down provisions that fixed a minimum age of fifty for appointment and four-year terms. Parliament then passed the Tribunals Reforms Act 2021, which contained provisions of similar effect. On 19 November 2025, in Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (2025 INSC 1330), a Bench of CJI B.R. Gavai and K. Vinod Chandran J. struck down key provisions of that Act, among those challenged being sections 3(1), 3(7), 4, 5, 6, 7(1) and 33. The Court said that the provisions “violate the constitutional principles of separation of powers and judicial independence”; that the Act “simply re-enacts them in another avatar”; and that “This amounts to a legislative override in the strictest sense”. As reported, the Court explained that Parliament may cure the defect which formed the basis of a judgment, but cannot nullify the judgment itself by enacting the same provisions again. The Union was given four months to establish a National Tribunals Commission, guided by independence from the executive, professional expertise, transparent processes and oversight. Members of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal appointed by orders of 11 September 2021 and 1 October 2021 remain governed by the older Act and rules, and appointments whose selection was completed before the Act were protected. The decision revives a long argument about who controls the institutions that decide disputes involving the State.
verbatim_extracts: violate the constitutional principles of separation of powers and judicial independence
simply re-enacts them in another avatar
This amounts to a legislative override in the strictest sense

questions.question: According to the passage, the legislature's power in relation to a judgment that struck down a law is best described as

options.A: a power to cure the defect that formed the basis of the judgment, but not to nullify the verdict by re-enacting the same provisions
options.B: a power to overrule the judgment by a simple majority, since Parliament is the superior law-making body
options.C: a power confined to legislating prospectively, and only after the Court has permitted it
options.D: a power to re-enact the struck-down provisions in identical words once the House has considered the Court's reasoning and recorded its disagreement

questions.explanation: The Court distinguished curing the basis of a judgment (permissible) from overriding the verdict (impermissible).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D would permit the very override condemned. Option B gives Parliament a power the Court denied. Option C adds a requirement of judicial permission that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: The correct answer is a two-sided rule; students often choose a one-sided answer favouring either Parliament or the Court.
questions.language_trick: 'cure' and 'nullify' mark the two sides.

questions.question: Under the directions on a National Tribunals Commission, the Union must

options.A: abolish all existing tribunals within four months and transfer their pending matters to the High Courts concerned
options.B: place the Commission under the administrative control of a Union Ministry until fresh legislation is passed
options.C: establish the Commission within four months, following principles of independence from the executive, professional expertise, transparency and oversight
options.D: seek the approval of this Court for each appointment that the Commission may recommend in future

questions.explanation: The direction is to set up the Commission within four months on stated principles.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A orders abolition, not creation. Option B puts the Commission under executive control, contrary to the independence principle. Option D adds a judicial approval step not found in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option is an extreme institutional design that looks like a possible remedy.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A tribunal member was appointed by an order dated 1 October 2021 under the new Act. On the passage, the member's service conditions

options.A: are to be reconsidered by the National Tribunals Commission after four months
options.B: continue to be governed by the older Act and rules, since the Court protected such appointments
options.C: are void from the date of appointment, since the whole Act was declared unconstitutional by the Court in 2025
options.D: are governed entirely by the struck-down provisions, which remain valid for those already appointed under the new Act

questions.explanation: The passage records that ITAT members appointed under the orders of 11 September and 1 October 2021 remain governed by the older Act and rules.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D keeps the struck-down law alive. Option A sends the matter to a body not yet established. Option C voids appointments that the Court protected.
questions.clat_trap: The student must apply a saving direction, not the general consequence of striking down.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) is relevant to the passage because it

options.A: struck down Articles 323A and 323B as inconsistent with the Preamble to the Constitution
options.B: held that the executive may fix the term and age of tribunal members by delegated rules
options.C: held that tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B may entirely exclude the jurisdiction of the High Courts and the Supreme Court in service matters
options.D: held that tribunal decisions remain subject to High Court review under Articles 226 and 227, treating judicial review as a basic feature

questions.explanation: The passage states that tribunal decisions remain open to High Court scrutiny and that judicial review is part of the basic structure.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C reverses the holding. Option A invents a striking down of the Articles. Option B supplies a proposition that the passage does not attribute to the case.
questions.clat_trap: A case name studied for another proposition invites a half-remembered answer.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The words 'in the strictest sense' in the Court's remark on legislative override suggest that the Court

options.A: regarded every later law on tribunals as an override of the earlier decisions on tribunals, whatever its content or purpose
options.B: saw the re-enactment as an override of the judgment itself and not merely a fresh attempt at legislating on the subject
options.C: approved the override because Parliament had considered the objections of the Court and recorded reasons for enacting the law again
options.D: treated the override as a technical lapse for which no consequences follow

questions.explanation: The intensifier shows that the case before the Court was the clearest form of override: the same provisions re-enacted.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns a precise criticism into a blanket one. Option D contradicts the striking down. Option C contradicts the decision.
questions.clat_trap: A single adverbial phrase carries the entire inference, and the wrong options either generalise or reverse it.
questions.language_trick: 'strictest' limits the criticism to the clearest category.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Court treated the re-enactment of the struck-down provisions as a legislative override. Reason (R): The Court struck the provisions down because Parliament has no power to legislate on tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is true, as the Court called it a legislative override. R is false because the provisions fell for violating separation of powers and judicial independence, not for lack of competence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is false and does not explain A.
questions.clat_trap: R sounds plausible because the passage opens with Articles 323A and 323B, but those Articles give Parliament power.
questions.language_trick: 'has no power' is a categorical statement of incompetence which the passage never makes.

passages.title: Entering the Judiciary: All India Judges Association (2025) and Rejanish K.V. v. K. Deepa (2025)
passages.passage: Entry into the subordinate judiciary has long been shaped by the Court's All India Judges' Association cases. The 1993 decision required three years' practice for entry-level judges. The Shetty Commission (1999) recommended dropping the condition, and the 2002 decision accepted that view, setting the District Judge recruitment ratio at 50:25:25. On 20 May 2025, a Bench of CJI B.R. Gavai, A.G. Masih and K. Vinod Chandran JJ. reversed course. As reported, the Court noted that judges “from the very day they assume service, deal with (matters of) life, liberty, property”. A candidate for Civil Judge (Junior Division) must now show three years' practice, or equivalent experience as a law clerk, counted from provisional enrolment with the State Bar Council and not from the AIBE result. The requirement operates from the next recruitment, not for processes already begun; High Courts must amend their rules within three months. The Court also raised the quota for promotion to District Judge through the limited departmental competitive examination from ten to twenty-five per cent. On 9 October 2025, in Rejanish K.V. v. K. Deepa (2025 INSC 1208), a five-judge Constitution Bench led by CJI Gavai considered Article 233(2), under which a person not already in the service is eligible for appointment as District Judge if he has been for at least seven years an advocate or pleader. The Bench held that in-service judicial officers may compete for the bar-quota posts, with the seven-year requirement met by combined experience as advocate and judicial officer, and a minimum age of thirty-five years. The Court said that “the plain meaning coming out of the words employed does not provide any restriction to judicial officers”. The decision disapproved the approach of Dheeraj Mor (2020), which had confined the quota to practising advocates. It applies prospectively.
verbatim_extracts: from the very day they assume service, deal with (matters of) life, liberty, property
the plain meaning coming out of the words employed does not provide any restriction to judicial officers

questions.question: A law graduate was provisionally enrolled with a State Bar Council in January 2022 and cleared the AIBE only in March 2025. A recruitment process for Civil Judge (Junior Division) is notified in July 2025. On the passage, the candidate

options.A: satisfies the condition only if the practice has been certified in person by a sitting Judge of the High Court
options.B: fails the condition, because a recruitment process notified in 2025 must follow the 2002 rule on fresh graduates
options.C: satisfies the experience condition, since practice is counted from provisional enrolment and not from the AIBE result, giving more than three years by the notification
options.D: fails the condition, because practice is counted only from the date of clearing the AIBE in March 2025

questions.explanation: Practice is counted from provisional enrolment; from January 2022 to July 2025 is more than three years.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reverses the counting rule. Option A invents a certification requirement. Option B applies the 2002 rule, which the 2025 decision reversed.
questions.clat_trap: Dates are given so that the student has to compute; the AIBE date is a deliberate distractor.
questions.language_trick: 'counted from' decides the starting point.

questions.question: The 2025 AIJA decision departs from the 2002 decision in that it

options.A: accepts the Shetty Commission's recommendation for the first time and removes the requirement of practice for entry into the lowest rung
options.B: restores the minimum-practice condition which the 2002 decision had dropped on the Shetty Commission's recommendation
options.C: fixes the District Judge recruitment ratio at 50:25:25 instead of earlier percentages
options.D: abolishes the limited departmental competitive examination as a route to District Judge

questions.explanation: The passage records that 2002 removed the condition and 2025 reinstated it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the sequence. Option C attributes the 2002 ratio to 2025. Option D reverses the LDCE change, since the quota was raised.
questions.clat_trap: The history is a sequence (1993, 1999, 2002, 2025), and wrong options rearrange it.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: An advocate-turned-judicial officer has four years at the Bar and four years in the judicial service and is thirty-eight years old. He applies for the bar-quota post of District Judge in a recruitment notified after October 2025. On the passage, he

options.A: is eligible, because the seven-year requirement in Article 233(2) may be met by combined experience as advocate and judicial officer and the age of thirty-five is satisfied
options.B: is eligible only if he had practised continuously as an advocate for seven years before joining the service
options.C: is ineligible, because a judicial officer is regarded as already in service and cannot be treated as an advocate for the quota
options.D: is ineligible, because Dheeraj Mor (2020) confined the quota to advocates practising on the date of the appointment

questions.explanation: Rejanish allows judicial officers to compete, counts combined experience, and sets a minimum age of thirty-five; Dheeraj Mor's approach was disapproved.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C and Option D restate the position the Constitution Bench disapproved. Option B demands pure practice, which the passage rejects.
questions.clat_trap: The hypothetical applies the new rule to a candidate on whom the older rule would have operated differently.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The quoted sentence from Rejanish mainly signifies that

options.A: the Constitution requires every District Judge to have served earlier as a judicial officer
options.B: the High Courts alone may decide whether judicial officers are eligible for the quota
options.C: the text of Article 233(2) does not itself exclude judicial officers
options.D: judicial officers are expressly preferred over advocates for the posts of District Judge

questions.explanation: The sentence is about plain textual meaning: the words contain no restriction on judicial officers.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D adds a preference which the text lacks. Option A imposes a different requirement. Option B transfers a constitutional question to High Courts.
questions.clat_trap: Short correct options can be overlooked when the wrong ones sound more impressive.
questions.language_trick: 'plain meaning' signals textual interpretation.

questions.question: On the passage, the temporal reach of the two 2025 decisions is that

options.A: recruitments already under way are not disturbed and High Courts must amend their rules within a stated period
options.B: neither decision requires any change in the rules of the High Courts
options.C: both decisions invalidate all appointments made earlier under conflicting rules
options.D: the AIJA decision is prospective while Rejanish applies to appointments already made under the earlier reading of Article 233

questions.explanation: The passage records prospective operation for both decisions and a three-month period for High Courts under the AIJA ruling.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C makes both retrospective. Option D splits them without basis. Option B denies the rule-making direction.
questions.clat_trap: 'Prospective' and 'retrospective' are interchanged in the wrong options.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements and select the correct combination.
I. The 2025 AIJA decision counts practice from the date of clearing the AIBE.
II. The 2025 AIJA decision raised the LDCE quota for District Judge from ten to twenty-five per cent.
III. Rejanish held that in-service judicial officers cannot compete for the bar-quota posts of District Judge.
IV. Rejanish operates prospectively.

options.A: I and III only
options.B: II and IV only
options.C: I, II and IV only
options.D: II, III and IV only

questions.explanation: II and IV match the passage. I is wrong because counting is from provisional enrolment. III reverses the holding.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: The other combinations include I or III, both of which are false.
questions.clat_trap: The counting rule and the eligibility rule are each reversed in a statement, so a partly accurate memory of either leads to a wrong option.
questions.language_trick: 'cannot compete' contradicts the quoted plain-meaning sentence.

passages.title: Can Courts Modify Arbitral Awards? Gayatri Balasamy v. ISG Novasoft (2025)
passages.passage: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, modelled on the UNCITRAL Model Law, allows recourse to a court against an award only through an application to set it aside under Section 34, with an appeal under Section 37. Judicial decisions, from McDermott International v. Burn Standard (2006) to Project Director, NHAI v. M. Hakeem (2021), had said that the power to set aside does not include a power to modify. The dispute in Gayatri Balasamy v. ISG Novasoft Technologies began in a challenge to an award of two crore rupees, which a single judge of the Madras High Court enhanced, and a Division Bench later reduced the enhancement. On 20 February 2024 a Bench observed that the Court had taken conflicting views in two streams of cases and referred the question to a larger Bench. A five-judge Constitution Bench headed by CJI Sanjiv Khanna reserved judgment on 19 February 2025 and delivered it on 30 April 2025 (2025 INSC 605). By a 4:1 majority it held that the Court “has a limited power under Sections 34 and 37 of the 1996 Act to modify the arbitral award”. That limited power covers severing the invalid part of an award from the valid part, and “correcting any clerical, computational or typographical errors which appear erroneous on the face of the record”; it extends in some circumstances to post-award interest. As reported, the majority added that Article 142 applies, but “the power must be exercised with great care and caution”. Where modification is uncertain, the Court should remand under Section 34(4), giving the tribunal a chance to remove the defect. Justice K.V. Viswanathan dissented, taking the view that Section 34 gives no power to modify or vary the arbitral award.
verbatim_extracts: has a limited power under Sections 34 and 37 of the 1996 Act to modify the arbitral award
correcting any clerical, computational or typographical errors which appear erroneous on the face of the record
the power must be exercised with great care and caution

questions.question: The position in Project Director, NHAI v. M. Hakeem (2021), as against the Constitution Bench decision, is that Hakeem

options.A: had applied Article 142 to allow substitution of an award by the Court, which the majority accepted
options.B: had recognised a power to modify an award in all cases of error, which the Constitution Bench cut down
options.C: had denied any power to modify an award under Section 34, an approach which the majority in the Constitution Bench did not follow
options.D: had decided that an arbitral award can be modified only by the Division Bench of a High Court

questions.explanation: The passage places Hakeem in the line of decisions denying a power to modify, while the majority recognised a limited power.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reverses Hakeem's holding. Option A invents a role for Article 142 in Hakeem. Option D makes up a forum rule.
questions.clat_trap: The correct answer needs the earlier case located on the correct side of the conflict.
questions.language_trick: 'did not follow' is more accurate than 'overruled', which the passage does not say.

questions.question: An award consists of two independent heads. The first is within the submission to the tribunal and the second is beyond it. A Court under Section 34 can, on the passage,

options.A: modify the invalid part by substituting the sum it considers just
options.B: set aside the whole award and ask the parties to begin arbitration again before a fresh tribunal
options.C: hold that the award stands as it is, because errors of jurisdiction cannot be examined
options.D: sever the invalid part from the valid part and leave the valid part standing

questions.explanation: Severability is one of the limited situations in which the power to modify is recognised.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores severability and is too drastic. Option A treats modification as substitution of the Court's view. Option C denies any examination of jurisdiction.
questions.clat_trap: The options differ in how much power they give the Court, and only the middle option corresponds to the limited power in the passage.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The award states the amount due as Rs 12,00,000, but the tribunal's own calculation on the face of the award is Rs 1,20,000. On the passage, the Court

options.A: may recompute the amount on its own view of the evidence
options.B: must set aside the entire award as it lacks coherence
options.C: may correct the typographical error
options.D: may only remand, since correction is open to the tribunal alone

questions.explanation: Clerical, computational or typographical errors apparent on the face of the record can be corrected.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is disproportionate. Option A permits re-appreciation of evidence, which the limited power does not cover. Option D denies the Court's recognised power.
questions.clat_trap: A simple application is placed among options that exaggerate or deny the power.
questions.language_trick: 'on the face of the record' defines the permitted category.

questions.question: The role of the remand route under Section 34(4), as described, is that it

options.A: is available only when the Court has already decided to sever the award and fix the amount
options.B: is preferred where the Court is uncertain whether it may modify, allowing the tribunal itself to remove the defect
options.C: is a power belonging to the High Court that may be exercised only under Article 142
options.D: replaces the setting aside of awards in all cases where the dispute is of a commercial nature

questions.explanation: The passage says that, where modification is uncertain, the Court should remand under Section 34(4).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the condition for remand. Option D generalises it beyond the passage. Option C ties it to Article 142 without basis.
questions.clat_trap: The remand route is given as a safety valve, and the wrong options turn it into something else.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Justice Viswanathan's dissent, as stated in the passage, rests chiefly on the view that

options.A: Article 142 must never be invoked in an arbitration matter
options.B: the High Courts, not the Supreme Court, should decide on modification of arbitral awards in appropriate cases
options.C: severability of awards is not recognised by the Model Law
options.D: the statute offers only setting aside and modification would vary the award itself

questions.explanation: The passage reports the dissent as the view that Section 34 gives no power to modify or vary the award.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states a position the passage does not attribute to the dissent. Option C and Option B are not mentioned.
questions.clat_trap: The dissent is reported in a single clause, and the wrong options invent other grounds.
questions.language_trick: 'no power to modify or vary' is a flat denial of power.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Constitution Bench recognised a limited power to modify arbitral awards under Sections 34 and 37. Reason (R): The 20 February 2024 reference order noted that the Court had taken conflicting views in two streams of cases.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are true; the conflict explains why the reference was made but does not itself explain the content of the majority's holding.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is accurate but is the reason for the reference, not for the holding.
questions.clat_trap: R is true and appears to supply a reason, so students choose the first option, forgetting that R explains the reference and not the answer.
questions.language_trick: 'conflicting views' explains why a larger Bench sat, not what it decided.

passages.title: Poetry, the Police and the Strong-Minded Reader: Imran Pratapgarhi v State of Gujarat (2025)
passages.passage: On 28 March 2025 a Bench of Abhay S. Oka and Ujjal Bhuyan, JJ. decided Imran Pratapgarhi v State of Gujarat (2025 INSC 410, Criminal Appeal No. 1545 of 2025). A Member of Parliament had posted a video of a mass-marriage ceremony with a poem playing in the background. An FIR was registered at Jamnagar under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including Section 196 (promoting enmity between groups), and the Gujarat High Court declined to quash it at that stage. The Supreme Court quashed the FIR and all proceedings based on it. The judgment, authored by Oka J., speaks in two registers. On procedure, the Court held that when information is furnished about a speech-related offence, the officer must first read or hear the words: “Reading of written words, or hearing spoken words will be necessary to determine whether the contents make out a case of …” a cognizable offence, and that this exercise does not amount to a preliminary inquiry. Section 173(3) of the BNSS separately confers a discretion to hold a preliminary inquiry where the offence carries imprisonment of three to seven years. On substance, the Court said that the effect of words must be judged “based on standards of reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous individuals”, not by those who feel insecure or who treat criticism as a threat. It added: “The police officers must abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals.” On free speech it observed: “Even if a large number of persons dislike the views expressed by another …” the right to express those views must be respected and protected, and it is “the duty of the Courts to step in and protect the fundamental rights.” It also noted: “Literature including poetry, dramas, films, stage shows, satire and art, make the life of human beings more meaningful.” In a line quoted widely in public debate, the Court said that “75 years into our republic, we cannot be seen to be so shaky on our fundamentals that mere recital of a poem …” or stand-up comedy can be treated as creating enmity between communities. The strong-minded standard has its own lineage: it was laid down in Ramesh v Union of India (1988), which dealt with a television serial. The 1951 First Amendment, which added ‘public order’ to Article 19(2) after Romesh Thappar (1950), had earlier been invoked to justify restraints in cases such as Kedar Nath Singh (1962).
verbatim_extracts: Reading of written words, or hearing spoken words will be necessary to determine whether the contents make out a case of
based on standards of reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous individuals
The police officers must abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals.
Even if a large number of persons dislike the views expressed by another
the duty of the Courts to step in and protect the fundamental rights
Literature including poetry, dramas, films, stage shows, satire and art, make the life of human beings more meaningful.
75 years into our republic, we cannot be seen to be so shaky on our fundamentals that mere recital of a poem

questions.question: According to the passage, when information about a speech-related offence is furnished to the police, the officer

options.A: must first read or hear the words in question to see whether a cognizable offence is made out, and this step is not a preliminary inquiry
options.B: must register the FIR first and examine the words only during investigation, because reading them is itself a forbidden preliminary inquiry under settled principles
options.C: may hold a preliminary inquiry for up to fourteen days in every speech case, since such cases form a special category
options.D: must seek the approval of a senior officer before even reading the words, because speech cases cannot be processed locally

questions.explanation: The Court required the officer to read or hear the words and said this does not amount to a preliminary inquiry. The separate discretion in Section 173(3) BNSS is limited to offences carrying three to seven years.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reverses the sequence the Court laid down and mislabels the reading of words. Option C invents a fixed inquiry period and makes it universal. Option D adds a layer of approval that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: Because the right answer calls the reading of words 'not a preliminary inquiry' while the wrong options use that very phrase, a hurried reader may confuse the two exercises. The trap lies in the difference between reading the words and a preliminary inquiry under Section 173(3).
questions.language_trick: The phrase 'does not amount to' in the right option is the key. The wrong options reuse 'preliminary inquiry' in the opposite sense.

questions.question: On the passage, the effect of allegedly offending words is to be judged by the standard of

options.A: the most sensitive member of the targeted community, since the harm of enmity is measured by the reaction of the weakest listener
options.B: the police officer receiving the complaint, whose subjective view of the likely reaction of the audience is decisive at the registration stage
options.C: reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous persons, and not of those who see danger in criticism
options.D: an average citizen of ordinary prudence who may be easily alarmed, since public order is a fragile condition in a plural society

questions.explanation: The Court rejected the standard of weak or wavering minds and adopted the strong-minded person test, which it traced to Ramesh v Union of India (1988).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A adopts the hypersensitive-listener standard the Court discarded. Option D imports an 'easily alarmed' citizen. Option B makes the officer's subjective view the test, which the Court did not accept.
questions.clat_trap: Three plausible-sounding standards invite a student to choose the one that matches the intuition of public order. The Court's test is deliberately objective and robust, not protective of fragile sentiment.
questions.language_trick: 'Strong-minded, firm and courageous' sets a high threshold; 'ordinary prudence' in a wrong option looks similar but is a different test.

questions.question: A stage satirist performs a sketch that many members of one community find distasteful, but the sketch contains no call to violence and no incitement to hatred. In the light of the Court's reasoning, a Section 196 BNS FIR against the satirist is

options.A: sustainable, because satire on a community falls outside poetry and art, which alone enjoy the protection described by the Court
options.B: unlikely to be sustained, because disliked views, satire and art are protected, and the words must be tested by a strong-minded standard before any enmity can be inferred, with the Court expected to step in to protect the right
options.C: unsustainable only if the satirist first obtains a certificate from a regulator that the sketch is not likely to disturb public order
options.D: sustainable, because the dislike of a large number of persons is sufficient to show that the sketch promotes enmity between groups

questions.explanation: The Court's reasoning protects disliked views, satire and art and sets a robust standard. A mere dislike by many persons does not make out Section 196.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D turns popular dislike into the offence, the opposite of the Court's holding. Option A wrongly limits the protection to poetry and art, though the Court named satire and stand-up comedy too. Option C invents a prior certification requirement.
questions.clat_trap: The long correct option and the unfamiliar facts make the question look harder than it is. The answer follows from reading 'satire' and 'dislike' in the quoted lines closely.
questions.language_trick: 'Even if a large number of persons dislike' answers the argument in the first wrong option directly. The words 'poetry, dramas, films, stage shows, satire and art' are a list, not a limit.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the relationship between the strong-minded person standard and earlier law, as described in the passage?

options.A: The First Amendment of 1951 created the standard when it added 'public order' to Article 19(2), and Ramesh later endorsed it
options.B: Kedar Nath Singh (1962) introduced the standard, and Imran Pratapgarhi overruled that decision on public order in the process
options.C: Ramesh v Union of India (1988) laid down the standard, and Imran Pratapgarhi applies it to Section 196 BNS
options.D: Romesh Thappar (1950) laid down the standard, and Imran Pratapgarhi extended it for the first time to criminal proceedings under the BNS

questions.explanation: The passage attributes the standard to Ramesh (1988) and says the 1951 amendment and Kedar Nath relate to public order restraints, not to the strong-minded test.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B credits the wrong case and invents an overruling. Option A confuses a constitutional amendment with a judicial standard. Option D credits a case that predates the test and ignores earlier criminal usage.
questions.clat_trap: A student who knows the 1951 amendment and Kedar Nath may link them with every free-speech standard. The passage keeps those two separate.
questions.language_trick: 'laid down' and 'applies it' in the right option describe origin and use, which the wrong options blur.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the passage?

options.A: Poetry and satire are protected only if a body of literary experts has approved the work before publication
options.B: Section 173(3) BNSS gives the officer a discretion to hold a preliminary inquiry in offences punishable with three to seven years
options.C: The Court saw the protection of fundamental rights as a duty resting on courts too
options.D: The Court quashed the FIR and all proceedings based on it, setting aside the High Court order

questions.explanation: Nothing in the passage requires prior approval by experts. The other statements are drawn from the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D, Option C and Option B each restate the passage, so they are consistent with it.
questions.clat_trap: The 'NOT' stem asks for the inconsistent statement, and the three true statements are written in measured language that tempts a student to look for a hidden flaw in them.
questions.language_trick: 'only if' and 'prior approval' signal an unfamiliar restriction that the passage never mentions.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Imran Pratapgarhi v State of Gujarat (2025).
I. The Court held that reading the words complained of is itself a preliminary inquiry that the police may not undertake.
II. The judgment was delivered by a Bench of Oka and Bhuyan, JJ., and authored by Oka J.
III. The Court observed that 75 years into the republic it cannot be so shaky on its fundamentals that the mere recital of a poem is treated as creating enmity.
IV. The Court declined to quash the FIR and left the matter to be decided at trial.
Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and IV only
options.C: II and III only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements II and III are drawn from the passage. Statement I contradicts the holding that reading the words is not a preliminary inquiry, and statement IV contradicts the quashing of the FIR.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A includes the incorrect statement I. Option B includes the incorrect statement IV. Option D contains two incorrect statements.
questions.clat_trap: Statement I is a deliberate inversion of the actual holding, placed first so that it feels like the 'main point' of the case.
questions.language_trick: 'itself a preliminary inquiry' is the inverted phrase; the Court said the reading 'does not amount to' one.

passages.title: Decency, Disability and the Regulation of Online Speech: the Allahabadia Litigation (2025-2026)
passages.passage: The India's Got Latent episode of early 2025 produced FIRs against several comedians and a podcaster in different States, and Ranveer Gautam Allahabadia v Union of India (W.P. (Crl.) No. 83 of 2025) reached the Supreme Court on a plea to club them. Connected petitions, including Cure SMA Foundation of India v Union of India (W.P. (C) No. 460 of 2025), complained of demeaning remarks about persons with disabilities. Obscenity law has an old lineage. English law's Hicklin test (1868) asked whether matter tended to deprave and corrupt those open to such influences; Indian courts followed it in Ranjit Udeshi v State of Maharashtra (1965), and Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal (2014) replaced it with a community standards test. Article 19(2) permits restrictions in the interests of ‘decency or morality’, and Ajay Goswami v Union of India (2007) accepted that regulation of material harmful to minors must be balanced against adult speech. On 27 November 2025 a Bench of CJI Surya Kant and Joymalya Bagchi, JJ. heard the matters. The reported oral remarks included: “Self styled bodies will not help..some neutral autonomous bodies.” The CJI asked why violations kept recurring if self-regulation was effective, and said: “We will not put our seal of approval on something which can gag somebody.” The written order recorded the Attorney General's information that the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting was proposing guidelines and inviting public suggestions, and listed the matter after four weeks. During the hearing the Bench altered a reference to a ‘preventive’ mechanism to an ‘effective’ one after counsel raised the concern of pre-censorship. On 14 July 2026 the Court imposed costs of Rs 3 lakh on each of five comedians for what it found was a brazen violation of undertakings given to it. According to an account by the Internet Freedom Foundation (an advocacy group; verify against the signed order), the Court on 14 August 2026, in an order under Article 142, quashed the FIRs and closed the criminal petitions, found ‘true compliance’ with the undertakings, and stated in paragraph 15 that the larger issues on regulating speech on social media “can be taken up by this Court in another appropriate case.”
verbatim_extracts: Self styled bodies will not help..some neutral autonomous bodies.
We will not put our seal of approval on something which can gag somebody.
can be taken up by this Court in another appropriate case

questions.question: The remark that 'Self styled bodies will not help..some neutral autonomous bodies' is best classified, on the passage, as

options.A: a binding direction under Article 141 requiring the Centre to legislate an autonomous regulator within four weeks
options.B: an oral observation made at a hearing, not a direction in the order
options.C: a finding in the final order that self-regulation by industry bodies is unconstitutional under Article 19(2)
options.D: a ratio decidendi on which later benches are bound to rely when they examine the regulation of online content

questions.explanation: The passage reports it among the oral remarks of 27 November 2025, while the written order only recorded the proposal to frame guidelines and the listing after four weeks.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns an oral remark into a mandamus. Option C attributes a finding of unconstitutionality that is nowhere stated. Option D treats an observation as a binding ratio.
questions.clat_trap: Students tend to treat widely reported judicial remarks as holdings. The question tests the line between obiter remarks at a hearing and the operative order.
questions.language_trick: 'reported oral remarks' in the passage is the cue; 'direction', 'finding' and 'ratio' in the wrong options claim a status the remark lacks.

questions.question: A film-maker is prosecuted for a scene that a section of the audience finds vulgar, though it has no tendency to deprave in the old sense and fits what contemporary society tolerates. Applying the lineage described in the passage, the court would ask

options.A: whether the scene offends contemporary community standards judged as a whole, as Aveek Sarkar requires, rather than whether it might deprave the most susceptible viewer under the Hicklin test, which has been replaced
options.B: whether the scene could deprave and corrupt the most susceptible viewer, since the Hicklin test of 1868 continues to govern obscenity under Ranjit Udeshi
options.C: whether the scene offends the film-maker's own undertakings to the Court, since obscenity is determined by the undertakings given by the accused
options.D: whether the scene was approved by a self-regulatory body, since the Court has held that such approval is conclusive of decency

questions.explanation: Aveek Sarkar (2014) replaced the Hicklin test, which Ranjit Udeshi (1965) had adopted, with a community standards test.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B applies a test the passage says was replaced. Option D treats self-regulatory approval as conclusive, contrary to the remarks on self-regulation. Option C confuses a contempt-type question about undertakings with the test of obscenity.
questions.clat_trap: The longer correct option and the apparent link of Ranjit Udeshi with Hicklin invite the student to pick the older test.
questions.language_trick: 'replaced' and 'continues to govern' are opposite statements of the same history.

questions.question: According to the account of the order of 14 August 2026 given in the passage, the Court

options.A: declared that Article 21 must prevail over Article 19 and directed the creation of a statutory autonomous regulator for online content
options.B: framed binding guidelines for an influencer code and directed the Union to notify them within eight weeks of the order
options.C: quashed the FIRs under Article 142 and left the larger question of regulating speech on social media for another appropriate case
options.D: held that the five comedians had violated their undertakings and quashed the FIRs as a penalty on the complainants

questions.explanation: The passage says the Court quashed the FIRs, closed the criminal petitions and left the larger regulatory issue for another case.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B says guidelines were framed, but paragraph 15 left the issue open. Option D contradicts the finding of 'true compliance' in August. Option A combines an oral remark with an order that the passage does not report.
questions.clat_trap: Three months after the costs order, a student may recall the 'violation' and assume the final order was punitive; the later order records compliance.
questions.language_trick: 'quashed ... left ... another appropriate case' versus 'framed' or 'directed' is the difference between disposal and regulation.

questions.question: The costs of Rs 3 lakh on each of the five comedians in July 2026 were imposed for

options.A: the filing of multiple FIRs in different States, which the Court treated as an abuse of process by the complainants
options.B: the failure to secure prior certification of the episode from a content regulator
options.C: the violation of undertakings given to the Court, and not for the obscenity of the original remarks
options.D: the finding that the remarks in the episode were obscene under the community standards test of Aveek Sarkar

questions.explanation: The passage ties the costs to the brazen violation of undertakings given to the Court.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D assumes a finding on obscenity that the passage does not contain. Option B refers to a certification regime that does not exist. Option A penalises complainants, whereas the costs fell on the comedians.
questions.clat_trap: A student tends to connect the penalty with the original content because it received the most public attention. The passage ties it to a separate wrong: the breach of undertakings.
questions.language_trick: 'for what it found was a brazen violation of undertakings' places the wrong in the conduct before the Court.

questions.question: The Bench's alteration of 'preventive mechanism' to 'effective mechanism' in the November 2025 order is best understood as

options.A: a direction that the Ministry must create a statutory regulator, which a preventive mechanism barred
options.B: a response to pre-censorship concerns, showing the Court would not approve screening speech before publication
options.C: an acceptance of the Attorney General's argument that a pre-publication licence is constitutionally mandatory for creators
options.D: a decision that the mechanism must operate only after publication and must never involve any age verification of viewers

questions.explanation: The passage says the Bench changed the word after counsel raised the concern of pre-censorship. The Court's remark that it would not put its seal of approval on something that can gag somebody fits that reading.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reads a rule about age verification into the change, which the passage does not state. Option C reverses the direction of the concern. Option A invents a direction to create a statutory regulator.
questions.clat_trap: A subtle change of one word is made to carry too large a meaning in the wrong options. The answer rests on the reason stated in the passage.
questions.language_trick: 'pre-censorship' is the stated reason; the wrong options overstate what the amendment decided.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The oral remarks of the Bench in November 2025 on an autonomous regulator for online content can be cited as a holding that the State must create such a regulator.
Reason (R): The order of August 2026, as described in the passage, stated that the larger issues of regulating speech on social media can be taken up in another appropriate case.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The oral remarks were not a holding, so the assertion is false. The reason is true as described in the passage and itself shows that the larger question remained open.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A fails because oral remarks are not holdings. Therefore the pairings that call A true are incorrect.
questions.clat_trap: R is true and looks like support for A because both speak about regulation, so a student may link them as cause and effect.
questions.language_trick: 'can be cited as a holding' is the false claim.

passages.title: Grounds of Arrest in Writing: Mihir Rajesh Shah v State of Maharashtra (2025)
passages.passage: Article 22(1) of the Constitution provides that no person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest, and without the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice. For decades the question was how, and in what form, the grounds must be communicated. Pankaj Bansal v Union of India (2023) required written grounds in a prosecution under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, and Prabir Purkayastha v State (NCT of Delhi) (2024) did so under the UAPA, leaving it unclear whether ordinary offences were covered. In Mihir Rajesh Shah v State of Maharashtra (2025 INSC 1288), decided on 6 November 2025 by a Bench of CJI B.R. Gavai and Augustine George Masih, J., with the judgment authored by Masih J., the Court answered the question for arrests generally. The case arose from a high-profile hit-and-run incident in Mumbai. The Bombay High Court acknowledged procedural lapses in the arrest but declined to declare it illegal, citing the gravity of the offence and the alleged attempts to evade custody; the Supreme Court declared the arrest illegal. The Court held: “The grounds of arrest must be communicated in writing to the arrestee in the language he/she understands.” It said the requirement is “mandatory in all offences under all statutes”, and that the right under Article 22(1) “is not a mere formality but a mandatory binding constitutional safeguard.” On language, the Court observed that “The failure to supply such grounds in a language understood by the arrestee renders the constitutional safeguards illusory.” Where the grounds cannot practically be given in writing at the time of arrest, for example in cases such as offences against body or property committed in flagrante delicto, the arresting officer may convey them orally at that time, but the written grounds must follow “within a reasonable time and in any case at least two hours prior to production of the arrestee for remand proceedings before the magistrate.” Non-compliance renders the arrest and the subsequent remand illegal, and the arrestee may be set free, though a later remand application must explain any delay. Section 47 of the BNSS now carries the statutory duty to inform the arrestee of the grounds.
verbatim_extracts: The grounds of arrest must be communicated in writing to the arrestee in the language he/she understands.
mandatory in all offences under all statutes
is not a mere formality but a mandatory binding constitutional safeguard.
The failure to supply such grounds in a language understood by the arrestee renders the constitutional safeguards illusory.
within a reasonable time and in any case at least two hours prior to production of the arrestee for remand proceedings before the magistrate.

questions.question: Where the grounds of arrest are conveyed orally at the time of arrest because writing is impracticable, the passage requires that the written grounds be supplied

options.A: at the first hearing of bail, since the written grounds are meant to let the arrestee plead for release at that stage
options.B: only if the arrestee or his lawyer demands them in writing at the remand hearing before the Magistrate
options.C: within twenty-four hours of the arrest, which is the constitutional limit for production before the Magistrate in any event
options.D: within a reasonable time and at least two hours before the arrestee is produced before the Magistrate for remand

questions.explanation: The Court fixed the two-hour rule before production for remand, and the oral conveyance at arrest is an exception.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C borrows the twenty-four hour rule of Article 22(2), which is a different requirement. Option B makes the duty depend on a demand. Option A postpones supply to the bail stage, which would defeat its purpose.
questions.clat_trap: Twenty-four hours is a figure that every student associates with Article 22. The two-hour rule is a separate, shorter requirement.
questions.language_trick: 'at least two hours prior to production' sets a minimum interval before the remand hearing, not a maximum after the arrest.

questions.question: What is the consequence of non-compliance with the written grounds requirement, according to the passage?

options.A: the arrest becomes illegal but the remand remains valid because the Magistrate applies his own mind independently
options.B: the arrest and the subsequent remand are rendered illegal
options.C: the arrest stands, but the Magistrate must record the lapse and may release the accused only on conclusion of the investigation
options.D: the arrest is valid but the evidence collected during the custody becomes inadmissible at the trial of the accused

questions.explanation: The passage states that non-compliance renders the arrest and the subsequent remand illegal.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C turns the consequence into a mere record of a lapse. Option D invents an exclusionary rule. Option A splits the arrest and the remand, though the passage says both fall.
questions.clat_trap: The right option is the briefest and the wrong options add procedural-sounding qualifications that a careful exam candidate is tempted to prefer.
questions.language_trick: 'and the subsequent remand' joins two things that wrong option three separates.

questions.question: The significance of Mihir Rajesh Shah in relation to Pankaj Bansal and Prabir Purkayastha is that it

options.A: confines the requirement of written grounds to offences punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more under the general criminal law
options.B: overrules those decisions because they confined the requirement to money laundering and terrorism and thus created an arbitrary classification
options.C: holds that Article 22(1) applies only to arrests made under special statutes, while the BNSS provides separately for ordinary offences
options.D: extends the written-grounds requirement from special statutes to all offences under all statutes

questions.explanation: Those cases required written grounds under the PMLA and UAPA. Mihir Shah extended the requirement to all offences under all statutes.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B claims an overruling that the passage does not state. Option A narrows the rule by an invented threshold. Option C reverses the scope.
questions.clat_trap: A student who remembers the earlier cases as 'special statute cases' may think the new case is another special statute case.
questions.language_trick: 'extends' is the crucial verb; 'overrules' and 'confines' distort the relationship.

questions.question: X is arrested by the police at 10 a.m. for theft. An officer reads out the grounds in English, though X understands only Marathi. At 1.30 p.m. the written grounds, in English, are handed over, and X is produced before the Magistrate at 2 p.m. On the passage, the arrest and the remand are

options.A: valid, because oral grounds were conveyed at the time of arrest and the written grounds were supplied before the remand hearing began
options.B: illegal, because the written grounds were neither in a language X understands nor given at least two hours before production
options.C: valid, because theft is a property offence committed in flagrante delicto, which dispenses with written grounds
options.D: illegal only if X proves that he suffered prejudice from the absence of a Marathi translation at the remand hearing

questions.explanation: The language requirement and the two-hour rule are both violated, so the arrest and remand are illegal. The in flagrante exception allows oral grounds at the time of arrest but not the dispensing of written grounds.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores both the language and the two-hour interval. Option C misreads the exception as dispensing with written grounds. Option D imports a prejudice requirement that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: The facts give three separate cues (oral, language, timing), and a student who notices only one is drawn to the first option.
questions.language_trick: 'at least two hours prior' is measured to production, so 1.30 to 2.00 falls short.

questions.question: The Bombay High Court's reasoning for declining to declare the arrest illegal was rejected because

options.A: the High Court is not empowered to declare an arrest illegal in a case where the accused is alleged to have evaded the process of arrest
options.B: the High Court had not recorded that the arrest was made after notice to the arrestee under the BNSS
options.C: the gravity of the offence and the accused's attempts to evade custody cannot dilute a safeguard flowing from Articles 21 and 22(1)
options.D: the Supreme Court held that serious offences require a stricter standard of communication of grounds than other offences, given the greater loss of liberty

questions.explanation: The passage records that the High Court admitted procedural lapses but declined to act because of gravity and alleged evasion, and the Supreme Court declared the arrest illegal on the footing that the safeguard is mandatory.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invents a limit on the High Court's powers. Option D reverses the logic by making gravity heighten the rule instead of leaving the safeguard intact. Option B refers to a notice requirement that the passage does not discuss.
questions.clat_trap: The gravity of the offence is an emotive factor, and a student may prefer an option that says serious cases need more, not less, scrutiny.
questions.language_trick: 'cannot dilute' states that the safeguard is not scaled to the gravity of the offence.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Mihir Rajesh Shah v State of Maharashtra (2025).
I. The judgment was authored by Masih J. on a Bench with CJI Gavai.
II. The written grounds may be dispensed with in all cases of offences committed in flagrante delicto.
III. The Court described the right to be informed of the grounds as not a mere formality but a mandatory binding constitutional safeguard.
IV. The Court held that the requirement applies only to offences under the PMLA and the UAPA.
Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I and III only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: I, II and IV only
options.D: III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and III restate the passage. II is wrong because written grounds must follow the oral conveyance, and IV is wrong because the Court extended the rule to all offences under all statutes.
