questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B includes II, which misreads the exception. Option C includes II and IV, both incorrect. Option D includes IV, which states the earlier position and not the holding in this case.
questions.clat_trap: Statement IV states what the law was before the case and is placed to catch a student who remembers only the earlier decisions.
questions.language_trick: 'only to offences under the PMLA and the UAPA' contradicts 'all offences under all statutes'.

passages.subject_area: Criminal Procedure and Special Laws (PMLA and BNSS)
passages.title: Hearing Before Cognizance: Kushal Kumar Agarwal v Directorate of Enforcement (2025) and Parvinder Singh (2026)
passages.passage: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, a Magistrate who took cognizance on a complaint examined the complainant and witnesses under Section 200 and decided whether to issue process, without hearing the accused. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 changed this for complaints through Section 223. Its first proviso says that “no cognizance of an offence shall be taken by the Magistrate without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard.” The question was whether the proviso applies to a complaint made by the Enforcement Directorate under Section 44(1)(b) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. In Kushal Kumar Agarwal v Directorate of Enforcement (2025 INSC 760, Criminal Appeal No. 2749 of 2025), decided on 9 May 2025 by a Bench of Abhay S. Oka and Ujjal Bhuyan, JJ., the Court, relying on Yash Tuteja v Union of India (2024) and Tarsem Lal v Directorate of Enforcement (2024), held that such a complaint “will be governed by Sections 200 to 204 of the CrPC”. It followed that “Section 223 of the BNSS will apply to the present complaint”, which had been filed after the BNSS came into force on 1 July 2024. The Court said that “The proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 223 puts an embargo on the power of the Court to take cognizance …” without a hearing. The Special Judge had not given the appellant an opportunity of being heard, and the cognizance order was set aside only for that non-compliance, with no view on the merits. The appellant was directed to appear before the Special Court on 14 July 2025 for a hearing. The Court left open two submissions of the Additional Solicitor General: that the hearing is limited to the complaint and its documents, and that no fresh hearing is needed for a supplementary complaint. On 19 May 2026, in Parvinder Singh v Directorate of Enforcement (2026 INSC 519), a Bench of M.M. Sundresh and N. Kotiswar Singh, JJ. is reported to have held the proviso to be substantive and mandatory, so that cognizance taken without a hearing is void ab initio. There, the complaint was filed on 24 June 2024, before the BNSS, but cognizance was taken on 2 July 2024. The Court is reported to have held that merely numbering the complaint and fixing a date was not an ‘inquiry’ so as to attract the savings clause, set aside the cognizance order, and rejected a plea to reconsider Kushal Kumar Agarwal (verify the exact reasoning against the judgment).
verbatim_extracts: no cognizance of an offence shall be taken by the Magistrate without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard.
will be governed by Sections 200 to 204 of the CrPC
Section 223 of the BNSS will apply to the present complaint
The proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 223 puts an embargo on the power of the Court to take cognizance

questions.question: According to the passage, Section 223 BNSS applied to the ED complaint in Kushal Kumar Agarwal because

options.A: the PMLA expressly adopts Section 223 BNSS as part of its own self-contained procedure for the trial of money-laundering cases
options.B: the Court held that every accused in a special statute case must be heard before process is issued
options.C: a complaint under Section 44(1)(b) PMLA is governed by Sections 200 to 204 CrPC, so the corresponding BNSS provisions apply to a complaint filed after 1 July 2024
options.D: the complaint was filed by the Directorate, which is a Union agency whose complaints are treated as police reports under the BNSS and so follow a separate statutory route

questions.explanation: The Court reasoned that the PMLA complaint procedure falls under the CrPC's complaint chapter, so its BNSS counterpart applies to complaints after 1 July 2024.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A attributes an adoption to the PMLA that the passage does not mention. Option B overstates the hearing into a merits hearing. Option D calls the ED complaint a police report, which is a different route.
questions.clat_trap: The ordinary instinct is to look for a specific textual link in the PMLA. The link in the passage is through the CrPC's complaint procedure.
questions.language_trick: 'is governed by' sets the CrPC route as the mechanism of application.

questions.question: The Court in Kushal Kumar Agarwal set aside the cognizance order

options.A: only for non-compliance with the proviso, expressing no view on the merits, and directed the appellant to appear for a hearing before the Special Court
options.B: on the merits of the allegations, because the complaint did not disclose an offence of money laundering against the appellant
options.C: and quashed the complaint altogether, because the Special Judge had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of any PMLA complaint after the BNSS came into force
options.D: and directed that a fresh complaint be filed, because the earlier complaint was filed before the Special Court without sanction

questions.explanation: The order records that the setting aside rested only on the breach of the proviso and that the Court expressed no view on the merits.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B brings in merits, which the Court expressly avoided. Option C quashes the complaint, while the Court only set aside the cognizance order. Option D introduces a sanction requirement that the passage never mentions.
questions.clat_trap: A procedural victory is often read as a substantive one. The passage insists that the Court left the merits untouched.
questions.language_trick: 'only for' and 'expressing no view' limit the scope of the order.

questions.question: In Parvinder Singh (2026), as described, the complaint was filed on 24 June 2024 and cognizance was taken on 2 July 2024. Section 223 BNSS was held to apply because

options.A: the savings clause applies whenever the ECIR was registered before the BNSS began, whatever happens in court
options.B: the hearing right in Section 223 applies only to complaints filed by private persons and not to complaints made by public agencies
options.C: the complaint was filed before 1 July 2024, so the old CrPC applies and the accused has no hearing right at the cognizance stage
options.D: cognizance was taken after the BNSS came into force and no 'inquiry' had begun that could attract the savings clause

questions.explanation: On the reported reasoning, the date of cognizance and the absence of an 'inquiry' decided the point, and numbering a complaint and fixing a date was not an inquiry.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C uses the filing date, which the Court did not treat as decisive. Option A makes the ECIR date decisive, which the passage does not support. Option B restricts the right by complainant type, which has no basis in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Facts with two dates around 1 July 2024 are meant to confuse a student about which date matters. The question turns on the act of taking cognizance.
questions.language_trick: 'cognizance was taken after' fixes the date that counts.

questions.question: A Special Judge, after hearing the accused as required by the proviso, takes cognizance of an ED complaint. The ED later files a supplementary complaint, and the Special Judge takes cognizance of it without a fresh hearing. On the passage, the accused's objection that a fresh hearing was mandatory is

options.A: bound to succeed, since the proviso makes a hearing mandatory before every act of taking cognizance, and a supplementary complaint is no exception
options.B: irrelevant, since the proviso applies only where the Magistrate takes cognizance on a police report and not on a complaint filed by an agency
options.C: bound to fail, since the Court held that the hearing under the proviso is limited to the first complaint and its documents alone
options.D: a point that Kushal Kumar Agarwal left open for the Special Court to decide, so the passage does not settle it in the accused's favour or against him

questions.explanation: The passage records that the Court left open the submission that no fresh hearing is needed for a supplementary complaint, so the matter is not settled by that decision.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats an open question as settled for the accused. Option C treats it as settled against him. Option B contradicts the holding that the proviso applies to the ED complaint.
questions.clat_trap: The two options that predict a clear result are attractive because the exam rewards decisiveness. The passage requires the answer 'left open'.
questions.language_trick: 'left open' and 'does not settle' are the safest descriptions of a matter the Court expressly reserved.

questions.question: The proviso to Section 223(1) BNSS is best described, on the passage, as

options.A: a right that matures only after the charge is framed
options.B: a precondition to the Court's taking cognizance
options.C: a directory guideline whose breach is curable at trial
options.D: a matter of discretion for the Special Judge in each case

questions.explanation: The Court said the proviso puts an embargo on the power to take cognizance without hearing, and the later case describes it as substantive and mandatory.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C calls it directory, which contradicts 'embargo'. Option A moves the right to charge stage. Option D makes it discretionary, which contradicts 'mandatory'.
questions.clat_trap: The short correct option is the least elaborate, and a student who looks for the most detailed answer will skip it.
questions.language_trick: 'embargo' in the quotation is a word of prohibition and not of guidance.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A Special Judge who takes cognizance of an ED complaint filed after 1 July 2024 without hearing the accused acts contrary to a mandatory provision of the BNSS.
Reason (R): The proviso to Section 223(1) BNSS puts an embargo on the power of the Court to take cognizance without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are consistent with the passage, and the reason is the textual ground for the assertion.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is wrong because R is the very ground for A. Options C and D are wrong because both statements are true.
questions.clat_trap: Students often expect an Assertion-Reason item on a subtle procedural point to hide a falsehood. Here both statements are correct.
questions.language_trick: 'embargo' in R is the exact word used by the Court.

passages.subject_area: Criminal Law and Constitutional Law (Curative Jurisdiction)
passages.title: Same Evidence, Opposite Outcomes: Surendra Koli v State of Uttar Pradesh (2025)
passages.passage: In December 2006, human remains were found near a house in Nithari village in Noida, and the case against Moninder Singh Pandher and his domestic help Surendra Koli grew into thirteen prosecutions. Koli was sentenced to death, and the Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and sentence in Surendra Koli v State of U.P. (2011), dismissed a review in 2014, and in January 2015 the High Court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment (verify the exact case in which commutation took place). On 16 October 2023 the High Court acquitted him in twelve companion prosecutions, and on 30 July 2025 the Supreme Court dismissed the State's appeals against those acquittals. The remaining conviction, in the thirteenth case (the Rimpa Haldar case), stood on the same kind of evidence: a confession recorded under Section 164 CrPC and discoveries claimed under Section 27 of the Evidence Act. On 11 November 2025 a Bench of CJI B.R. Gavai, Surya Kant and Vikram Nath, JJ., in a judgment authored by Nath J., allowed Koli's curative petition, recalled the 2011 decision and acquitted him. The curative petition is a judicial creation of Rupa Ashok Hurra v Ashok Hurra (2002), where a five-judge Bench held that a final judgment may be reopened after the dismissal of a review to prevent abuse of process and miscarriage of justice, in narrow circumstances such as a breach of natural justice; it rests on Article 142 and, in capital cases, on Mohd. Arif v Registrar (2014), which provides oral hearing of review petitions. According to reports of the judgment, the Court said: “The guiding principle for the exercise of curative jurisdiction is the duty of this Court to avert manifest injustice.” It added that “Arbitrary disparity in outcomes on an identical record is inimical to equality before the law”, that “The legal conclusion cannot change from case to case when the premise is identical”, and that “The curative jurisdiction exists to prevent precisely such anomalies from hardening into precedent.” On Section 27 it held that when the disclosure is not contemporaneously proved, the section ceases to operate. He was acquitted under Sections 302, 364, 376 and 201 IPC and ordered to be released unless required in another case.
verbatim_extracts: The guiding principle for the exercise of curative jurisdiction is the duty of this Court to avert manifest injustice.
Arbitrary disparity in outcomes on an identical record is inimical to equality before the law
The legal conclusion cannot change from case to case when the premise is identical
The curative jurisdiction exists to prevent precisely such anomalies from hardening into precedent.

questions.question: The principle on which the curative petition was allowed in Surendra Koli, according to the passage, was that

options.A: a curative petition operates as a second appeal that lets the Court re-appreciate evidence wherever the High Court has acquitted in others
options.B: the death sentence had been commuted in 2015, so the conviction in the thirteenth case had become inoperative by operation of law
options.C: the same evidence which had been rejected in twelve companion cases could not sustain a conviction in the thirteenth, as that would be manifest injustice
options.D: the earlier judgment of 2011 had been delivered without hearing the accused, in breach of natural justice, which is the only ground on which a curative petition lies in any case

questions.explanation: The Court relied on the arbitrary disparity between outcomes on an identical record, calling it manifest injustice.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D adopts a natural-justice ground that the passage does not mention here, and calls it the only ground. Option B invents a legal effect of commutation. Option A converts curative jurisdiction into a general appeal, which the passage rejects.
questions.clat_trap: The history of Rupa Ashok Hurra mentions natural justice, and a student may take that as the sole ground. The Koli decision applied manifest injustice to inconsistent outcomes.
questions.language_trick: 'only ground' in the first wrong option is an overstatement of Hurra, while 'manifest injustice' is the quoted principle.

questions.question: Which statement about the earlier phases of the litigation is consistent with the passage?

options.A: The Supreme Court dismissed the State's appeals against the twelve acquittals on 30 July 2025, before it recalled the 2011 decision in the thirteenth case
options.B: The High Court acquitted Koli in the thirteenth case on 16 October 2023 and the Supreme Court affirmed that acquittal in 2025
options.C: The Supreme Court affirmed the death sentence in 2011 and the High Court restored it in 2015 after a review of the mercy petition
options.D: The curative petition was filed before the State's appeals were dismissed and was heard by the same Bench that dismissed the review in 2014, according to the record

questions.explanation: The passage places the High Court's twelve acquittals in October 2023 and the Supreme Court's dismissal of the State's appeals in July 2025, followed by the curative decision in November 2025.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B places the acquittal in the wrong case. Option C reverses the 2015 commutation. Option D adds a procedural sequence and a Bench the passage does not state.
questions.clat_trap: A heavy timeline passage invites a student to rely on a loose memory of the sequence. The question tests the chronological order in the text.
questions.language_trick: 'twelve' and 'thirteenth' are the numbers that separate the two stages.

questions.question: The Court's reference to Section 27 of the Evidence Act, as described in the passage, shows that

options.A: a disclosure by an accused in custody is always admissible whether or not it leads to the discovery of any fact
options.B: discoveries are inadmissible in capital cases, whatever the evidence concerning the circumstances of the disclosure
options.C: the section applies only to confessions recorded by a Magistrate under Section 164 and not to statements made to the police
options.D: a discovery that is not contemporaneously proved cannot support a conviction

questions.explanation: The passage records that where the disclosure is not contemporaneously proved, Section 27 ceases to operate.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A stretches the section to all disclosures. Option C confuses Section 27 with Section 164 CrPC. Option B introduces a rule special to capital cases that the passage does not state.
questions.clat_trap: A concise answer hides inside longer options. The student has to hold the proof requirement in mind and not be pulled toward either of two extreme statements.
questions.language_trick: 'always' and 'whatever' in the wrong options are signals of overstatement.

questions.question: A convict's conviction in one case rests on a confession and discoveries that a competent court rejected as unreliable in twelve other cases arising from the same investigation, and his review petition has been dismissed. Applying the reasoning in the passage, the convict can invoke

options.A: a curative petition, as the identical record yields inconsistent outcomes that offend Articles 14 and 21 and amount to manifest injustice, and the Court may recall its earlier decision under Article 142
options.B: a second review petition, since a review may be filed repeatedly where the Court's earlier outcome is inconsistent with later findings on the same record
options.C: a fresh appeal on merits before a larger Bench, since the dismissal of a review always reopens the right of appeal in capital cases
options.D: only a mercy petition under Article 72, since the Court's power to reopen a final judgment is confined to cases of fraud on the Court

questions.explanation: The passage describes curative jurisdiction as available to prevent manifest injustice and links the disparity in outcomes to equality before the law and to Article 21.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B proposes repeated reviews that the Court does not allow. Option C claims a revived right of appeal. Option D restricts the power to fraud, which would exclude the Koli situation.
questions.clat_trap: The long correct option looks like a legal essay; the question is which remedy fits. The passage describes the curative remedy as the narrow route after the review is dismissed.
questions.language_trick: 'identical record' and 'inconsistent outcomes' map directly onto the quotations.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a correct statement about Rupa Ashok Hurra v Ashok Hurra (2002), as described in the passage?

options.A: It rests on the need to prevent abuse of process and miscarriage of justice
options.B: It permits a final judgment to be reopened after a review is dismissed, in narrow circumstances
options.C: It was decided by a five-judge Bench of the Supreme Court in 2002
options.D: It lets a curative petition precede the review decision

questions.explanation: The passage says a curative petition lies after the dismissal of a review, so the statement that it can be filed before review is decided is incorrect.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C, Option B and Option A reflect the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A negative stem makes a student look for the false statement among three accurate ones, and the false one differs by a single word about timing.
questions.language_trick: 'before a review petition is decided' reverses 'after the dismissal of a review'.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Surendra Koli v State of Uttar Pradesh (2025).
I. The judgment of 11 November 2025 was delivered by a Bench of CJI Gavai, Surya Kant and Vikram Nath, JJ.
II. The Court allowed the curative petition and recalled its 2011 decision in the thirteenth case.
III. The Court held that a curative petition may be used to re-appreciate evidence as in a second appeal.
IV. The Court acquitted Koli under Sections 302, 364, 376 and 201 IPC.
Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I and III only
options.B: I, II and IV only
options.C: II and III only
options.D: III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I, II and IV are consistent with the passage. Statement III is incorrect, since the object of curative jurisdiction is to cure a manifest miscarriage of justice and not to re-appreciate evidence as in a second appeal.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Options A, C and D include statement III, which misdescribes the curative jurisdiction.
questions.clat_trap: Statement III is the intuitive but wrong description of what a court does when it acquits on evidence.
questions.language_trick: 're-appreciate evidence as in a second appeal' contradicts the stated object of curative relief.

passages.title: Narco-Analysis and Voice Samples in 2025: Amlesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Rahul Agarwal v. State of West Bengal
passages.passage: Article 20(3) says that no person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. Two judgments of 2025 show how far the Supreme Court is willing to carry that guarantee into the investigator's laboratory. In Amlesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2025 INSC 810, 9 June 2025), Sanjay Karol and Prasanna B. Varale JJ. dealt with a dowry-harassment case in which the wife could not be traced. While hearing a bail plea, the Patna High Court accepted a police officer's submission that she would conduct narco-analysis tests on all the accused and other witnesses if required. The Supreme Court set that order aside. Relying on Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), a three-judge decision that held involuntary narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping to violate Articles 20(3) and 21, it repeated that “no individual should be forcibly subjected to any of the techniques in question.” It added that “there is no indefeasible right with the accused to undergo a narcoanalysis test”, although an accused may volunteer at an appropriate stage, and it held that a voluntary report “cannot form the sole basis of conviction of an accused person.” Information discovered as a result remains admissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act. The Court also quoted an earlier criticism that a High Court had “converted the adjudication of a bail matter to that of a mini trial indeed.” In Rahul Agarwal v. State of West Bengal (2025 INSC 1223, 13 October 2025), Chief Justice Gavai and K. Vinod Chandran J., the latter writing, reviewed an order of the Calcutta High Court that had set aside a Magistrate's direction to a witness to give a voice sample. The High Court had refused to follow Ritesh Sinha v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2019) because a reference to a larger bench was pending. The Supreme Court restored the Magistrate's order: “a Judicial Magistrate must be conceded the power to order a person, to give a sample of his voice”, and “with the advent of the BNSS, it has been specifically incorporated under Section 349.” Following State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961), an eleven-judge decision, such samples are treated as material rather than testimonial evidence, like fingerprints or handwriting.
verbatim_extracts: no individual should be forcibly subjected to any of the techniques in question
there is no indefeasible right with the accused to undergo a narcoanalysis test
cannot form the sole basis of conviction of an accused person
converted the adjudication of a bail matter to that of a mini trial indeed
a Judicial Magistrate must be conceded the power to order a person, to give a sample of his voice
with the advent of the BNSS, it has been specifically incorporated under Section 349

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the position on a voluntary narco-analysis test after Amlesh Kumar?

options.A: A Court may order the test over the objection of an accused who is charged with an offence punishable with life imprisonment
options.B: A voluntary test is a right of every accused who asks for it, and its report may be treated as substantive proof of guilt if safeguards are met
options.C: An accused may volunteer for it at an appropriate stage, but has no indefeasible right to demand it, and its report cannot alone sustain a conviction
options.D: No such test may ever be conducted, even at the accused's own request, because Selvi bars every technique of this kind

questions.explanation: Amlesh Kumar holds that there is no indefeasible right to the test, that voluntariness is the touchstone, and that even a voluntary report cannot be the sole basis of conviction.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B turns a permission into a right and treats the report as proof. Option D overstates Selvi, which left room for voluntary administration. Option A permits compulsion, which Articles 20(3) and 21 forbid.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option is a half-truth built on one familiar phrase from Selvi, so a student who remembers only 'narco-analysis is barred' is drawn to the second.
questions.language_trick: 'no indefeasible right' and 'cannot form the sole basis' are limits on a right and on evidence, not bans.

questions.question: The Court's remark that a High Court had 'converted the adjudication of a bail matter to that of a mini trial' is best read as criticism that the High Court

options.A: went beyond the limited inquiry proper to a bail application by sanctioning investigative steps against all the accused and other witnesses
options.B: passed its order without hearing the amicus curiae, which vitiated the direction for want of natural justice at the bail stage
options.C: decided the guilt of the accused while hearing bail, a task reserved to the Sessions Court only after the trial has been concluded and the evidence weighed fully
options.D: treated the narco-analysis report as admissible at the bail stage even though Selvi bars all use of such results as evidence

questions.explanation: The High Court accepted a police proposal to subject all accused, and witnesses, to narco-analysis in a bail matter. The Court saw that as an expansion of the bail inquiry into something resembling investigation or trial.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C says the High Court decided guilt, which it did not. Option B invents a procedural defect; the amicus was appointed in the Supreme Court. Option D wrongly says the report was admitted and overstates Selvi.
questions.clat_trap: The phrase 'mini trial' invites the guess that the High Court tried the accused; the real complaint is about scope.
questions.language_trick: 'mini trial' is a figure of speech for exceeding the narrow function of a bail inquiry.

questions.question: In Rahul Agarwal the Supreme Court's response to the High Court's reliance on a pending reference shows that

options.A: only the Supreme Court itself may notice a reference, so the High Court's order was void for want of jurisdiction
options.B: a pending reference to a larger bench does not suspend a binding decision, so the High Court should have continued to follow it
options.C: a High Court may set aside a binding decision for as long as any reference on the same point is pending before a larger bench of the Supreme Court
options.D: a reference to a larger bench overrules the earlier decision automatically from the date on which the reference is made

questions.explanation: The Court recorded that the High Court 'refused to follow the binding precedent' because of the reference, and restored the Magistrate's order on the basis of Ritesh Sinha, noting also that the reference had been closed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C is the very reasoning the Court rejected. Option D confuses a reference with an overruling. Option A invents a jurisdictional bar.
questions.clat_trap: A pending reference seems to cast doubt on the old rule, which is why the first wrong option is attractive.
questions.language_trick: 'binding precedent' and 'reference' pull in opposite directions; the stem asks which prevails while the reference is pending.

questions.question: A Magistrate directs a prosecution witness to give a voice sample for comparison with recorded calls. The witness objects under Article 20(3). On the two judgments, the objection

options.A: fails only if the witness is later named as an accused, since until then a sample can be taken solely with the witness's own consent
options.B: succeeds, because the Magistrate's power under the BNSS applies to accused persons only and does not extend to witnesses at all
options.C: fails, because a voice sample is material rather than testimonial evidence
options.D: succeeds, because protection against self-incrimination reaches any person called on to give evidence and a voice sample is a form of testimony

questions.explanation: The Court held that a Magistrate may order a sample from a person, not only an accused, and that a voice sample is physical or material evidence in the Kathi Kalu Oghad sense.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D treats a sample as testimony. Option B limits the power to accused persons, contrary to the Court's wording 'a person'. Option A invents a consent requirement tied to later accusation.
questions.clat_trap: The stem puts a witness in the dock of Article 20(3), which textually protects an 'accused'. Students therefore over-read the guarantee.
questions.language_trick: 'a person' in the quoted holding is wider than 'the accused'.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the passage?

options.A: Selvi held that involuntary narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping engage both Article 20(3) and Article 21
options.B: Voice samples are treated as material evidence in the way that fingerprints and handwriting are treated
options.C: Information discovered because of a voluntary test may still be admitted with the aid of section 27 of the Evidence Act
options.D: A narco-analysis test taken with consent can by itself prove guilt

questions.explanation: The passage says a voluntary report cannot form the sole basis of conviction. The statement in the stem contradicts it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C, Option A and Option B each restate the passage correctly.
questions.clat_trap: A negatively worded stem plus three true statements: the false one is the shortest and plainest.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT consistent' reverses the usual search; read the stem twice.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Magistrate's power to order a voice sample did not depend on section 349 of the BNSS. Reason (R): Ritesh Sinha had already conceded that power to a Judicial Magistrate even without an express provision in the earlier Code, and the BNSS later incorporated it.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Court noted that Ritesh Sinha conceded the power without an explicit Code provision and that section 349 BNSS later made it express. That history explains why the power did not depend on the new section.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R states the earlier source of the power and the later codification, so it explains A.
questions.clat_trap: Students may think a power needs a statutory source in force at the time, which the history of Ritesh Sinha answers.
questions.language_trick: 'did not depend on' is a statement about legal basis, not about whether the section exists.

passages.subject_area: Law of Evidence and Family Law (Presumption of Legitimacy)
passages.title: DNA Tests, Privacy and the Presumption of Legitimacy: R. Rajendran v. Kamar Nisha (2025)
passages.passage: Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 provides that birth during the continuance of a valid marriage is conclusive proof of legitimacy unless it is shown that the parties had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten. In R. Rajendran v. Kamar Nisha (2025 INSC 1304, 10 November 2025), Prashant Kumar Mishra and Vipul M. Pancholi JJ. decided what a criminal court may do when that presumption meets modern science. A married woman alleged that a doctor, who had referred her to his wife for fertility treatment, had a relationship with her; a child was born in 2007 and official records named her husband as the father. After she complained of cheating and harassment, the Madras High Court directed DNA profiling of the doctor, the woman and the child. The Supreme Court set the direction aside. Mishra J. described section 112 as one that “establishes a conclusive presumption in favour of legitimacy of a child born during the subsistence of a valid marriage.” The Court explained that “non-access denotes the impossibility, not merely the absence or lack of such opportunity.” It endorsed the test of “eminent need”, quoting Bhabani Prasad Jena (2010): “whether it is not possible for the Court to reach the truth without use of such test.” It added that “the best interests of the child ought to have been a paramount consideration before any intrusive forensic procedure was contemplated” and that “a direction for DNA testing must have a direct and demonstrable nexus with the offences under investigation.” The case sits within a long line. In Goutam Kundu v. State of West Bengal (1993) the Court warned against routine blood tests to prove paternity, and Nandlal Wasudeo Badwaik v. Lata Nandlal Badwaik (2014) let a DNA result prevail over the section 112 presumption. Puttaswamy (2017) later made bodily privacy a constitutional concern. The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 retains a corresponding presumption.
verbatim_extracts: establishes a conclusive presumption in favour of legitimacy of a child born during the subsistence of a valid marriage
Non-access denotes the impossibility, not merely the absence or lack of such opportunity
the best interests of the child ought to have been a paramount consideration before any intrusive forensic procedure was contemplated
A direction for DNA testing must have a direct and demonstrable nexus with the offences under investigation
eminent need
whether it is not possible for the Court to reach the truth without use of such test

questions.question: What does the Court mean by 'non-access' in relation to the presumption of legitimacy?

options.A: Impossibility of marital access during the period when the child could have been conceived, and not merely lack of opportunity
options.B: Any period of physical separation of the spouses, so that living apart for some months displaces the presumption automatically and without any proof
options.C: Failure of the husband to maintain the child, which shows that he does not accept paternity
options.D: The wife's own statement that her husband is not the father, which suffices to displace the presumption without further proof of any kind

questions.explanation: The Court said non-access denotes impossibility, not merely the absence or lack of opportunity. A strict standard is therefore applied before the presumption yields.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B equates separation with impossibility. Option D lets a spouse's allegation defeat a conclusive presumption. Option C invents a conduct-based test.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options mimic everyday notions of 'no access' and so lower the threshold.
questions.language_trick: 'not merely the absence or lack' sets a high bar.

questions.question: Why did the Court find the DNA direction against the doctor unsustainable?

options.A: A DNA test may be directed only in civil proceedings about paternity and never during an investigation into a criminal complaint
options.B: DNA evidence is inadmissible under the Evidence Act against a person who is not a party to the marriage in which the child was born
options.C: The presumption of legitimacy was not rebutted by proof of non-access, the paternity question lacked a direct nexus with the alleged offences, and the child's privacy and best interests had not been weighed
options.D: The High Court had failed to issue notice to the woman's husband, which alone vitiated the direction for want of a necessary party

questions.explanation: The Court set aside the High Court judgment because the presumption was unrebutted, the test lacked a necessary nexus with the offences, and privacy and the child's best interests had not been considered.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B invents an inadmissibility rule. Option D gives a procedural reason that is not the Court's. Option A imposes an absolute civil-only limit that the Court did not state.
questions.clat_trap: The correct option combines three reasons; each wrong option offers one clean, rule-like reason which sounds more 'legal'.
questions.language_trick: 'and' joins three conditions in the right option; none of the others is a stated ground.

questions.question: The 'eminent need' test applied by the Court was drawn from

options.A: Selvi (2010), which required the free consent of the person to be tested and a Magistrate's recorded satisfaction in every case
options.B: Puttaswamy (2017), whose four-limb test of legality, aim, proportionality and safeguards the Court quoted word for word here as the governing standard
options.C: Bhabani Prasad Jena (2010), which asks whether the truth can be reached without resort to the test, or the test is unavoidable
options.D: Nandlal Wasudeo Badwaik (2014), which made a DNA result prevail over the presumption in all disputes

questions.explanation: The Court's quotation at the relevant paragraph is attributed to Bhabani Prasad Jena. Badwaik, Puttaswamy and Selvi are in the background but are not the source of the 'eminent need' phrase.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D names the case that the passage cites for a different proposition. Option B claims a word-for-word quotation of Puttaswamy that the passage does not make. Option A imports the Selvi consent rule.
questions.clat_trap: Every option is a real case on the topic; only the attribution of the phrase is tested.
questions.language_trick: 'drawn from' asks for the source of the phrase, not for related authority.

questions.question: In the sentence 'Non-access denotes the impossibility, not merely the absence or lack of such opportunity', the words 'not merely' signal that

options.A: showing that the husband lacked an opportunity for access is insufficient without showing that access was impossible
options.B: proof that the husband was away for some months is enough, though more is preferable, before the presumption can be displaced
options.C: the presumption applies only where the spouses were living together at the time of conception, and not otherwise
options.D: the Court prefers a medical test to proof of non-access whenever the husband alleges that the child is not his own

questions.explanation: 'Not merely' raises the threshold: lack of opportunity is not enough; impossibility must be shown.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B turns 'not merely' into 'more is preferable'. Option D brings in medical tests, which the sentence does not mention. Option C limits the presumption to cohabitation.
questions.clat_trap: A small adverb changes the standard from opportunity to impossibility.
questions.language_trick: 'not merely' negates the weaker reading.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the passage?

options.A: The Court required a direct and demonstrable nexus between a DNA direction and the offences under investigation by the police
options.B: The Court held that a DNA test can never be ordered where the presumption of legitimacy arises
options.C: The Court stressed that the best interests of the child must weigh first before any intrusive forensic procedure is contemplated
options.D: The Court set aside the High Court's direction of 10 May 2017 for DNA profiling of the doctor, the woman and the child in this case

questions.explanation: The passage speaks of 'eminent need' and a nexus requirement, not an absolute ban. The statement in the stem overstates the holding.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D, Option C and Option A are each supported by the passage.
questions.clat_trap: 'never' is an absolute word; the Court's test is one of eminent need and nexus.
questions.language_trick: 'can never be ordered' contradicts the test of eminent need.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about R. Rajendran v. Kamar Nisha.
I. The Court described section 112 as establishing a conclusive presumption of legitimacy for a child born during a valid marriage.
II. The respondent alleged that the appellant, a doctor, was the child's biological father.
III. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's direction for DNA profiling of the appellant, the respondent and the child.
IV. The Court treated the child's best interests and privacy as relevant before any intrusive forensic procedure.
Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, II and IV only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I, II and IV match the passage. Statement III is false because the Supreme Court set the direction aside.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option 'I and II only' leaves out the privacy and best-interests point. The options with III treat the High Court direction as upheld, which is wrong.
questions.clat_trap: Statement III reverses the outcome; a student who remembers 'DNA test' may assume it was allowed.
questions.language_trick: 'upheld' versus 'set aside' decides statement III.

passages.subject_area: Constitutional Law (Article 21, Equality and Disability Rights)
passages.title: Digital Access and Accessible Examinations: Pragya Prasun/Amar Jain (2025) and Mission Accessibility v. Union of India (2025)
passages.passage: Aadhaar-based and video e-KYC now gate access to banking, wallets and welfare. In Pragya Prasun v. Union of India, heard with Amar Jain v. Union of India (30 April 2025), a bench of J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan JJ. considered petitions by acid-attack survivors and persons with visual impairment who could not complete KYC because the process demanded actions such as blinking on camera. R. Mahadevan J. wrote that “the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution must be re-interpreted in light of these technological realities”, that “the right to digital access therefore emerges as an instinctive component of the right to life and liberty”, and that “bridging the digital divide is no longer a matter of policy discretion but has become a constitutional imperative.” The State's obligation was said to arise under Article 21 read with Articles 14, 15 and 38. The directions included alternatives to the “blinking of eyes” liveness check, acceptance of thumb impressions, retention of paper-based KYC, accessibility audits of regulated entities, user testing with persons with blindness, compliance with WCAG 2.1 and GIGW standards, and grievance redress. The Court spoke of substantive equality, and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (which replaced the 1995 Act and follows the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities) supplied the statutory vocabulary of reasonable accommodation. In Mission Accessibility v. Union of India (2025 INSC 1376, 3 December 2025), Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta JJ., the latter writing, dealt with civil services examinations. The Court said the State “must therefore move beyond formal equality to ensure substantive inclusion”, and that a public body “must ensure that its processes are accessible, transparent, and sensitive to the needs of every segment of society.” It directed UPSC to permit candidates eligible for a scribe to request a change of scribe “up to at least seven days prior” to the examination, and to work with the disability department on protocols for screen-reader software. The line runs back to Vikash Kumar v. UPSC (2021), on scribes, to Rajive Raturi v. Union of India (2024), on accessibility, and to Anuradha Bhasin (2020), where access to the internet was tied to Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g).
verbatim_extracts: the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution must be re-interpreted in light of these technological realities
The right to digital access therefore emerges as an instinctive component of the right to life and liberty
Bridging the digital divide is no longer a matter of policy discretion but has become a constitutional imperative
must therefore move beyond formal equality to ensure substantive inclusion
must ensure that its processes are accessible, transparent, and sensitive to the needs of every segment of society
up to at least seven days prior

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT among the directions issued in the e-KYC judgment, as described in the passage?

options.A: Guidelines on alternatives to the 'blinking of eyes' liveness check for those who cannot perform it
options.B: Acceptance of thumb-impression images during the Digital KYC process by the regulated entities concerned
options.C: Periodic accessibility audits of regulated entities with user testing involving persons with blindness
options.D: Replacement of paper-based KYC by a fully digital route for all customers

questions.explanation: The Court retained paper-based KYC as an accessible alternative; it did not replace it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option B and Option C are listed directions.
questions.clat_trap: The false option is the shortest and sounds like the logical end of digitisation.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT' reverses the search; 'fully digital for all customers' is the opposite of the direction.

questions.question: How does the Court build a positive duty on the State from Article 21 in the digital context?

options.A: By holding that Article 21 restrains State action only, so that the digital divide remains a matter of executive policy which the Court may recommend but not require
options.B: By relying on Articles 14 and 15 alone, since Article 21 cannot be extended to technology-based services that did not exist in 1950
options.C: By treating Article 38 as a directive principle that becomes enforceable only through legislation, so the Court merely urged Parliament to act
options.D: By reading the State's obligation under Article 21 with Articles 14, 15 and 38, so that digital services must be made inclusive to realise substantive equality for those excluded by disability

questions.explanation: The passage records that the obligation arises under Article 21 read with Articles 14, 15 and 38 and that bridging the digital divide is a constitutional imperative.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts 'no longer a matter of policy discretion'. Option B excludes Article 21. Option C treats Article 38 as unenforceable, contrary to the Court's use of it.
questions.clat_trap: Directive principles are usually non-justiciable; the Court here uses Article 38 as an aid to interpret Articles 14 and 21.
questions.language_trick: 'positive duty' in the stem requires an obligation to act, not mere restraint.

questions.question: A bank's video-KYC app rejects an acid-attack survivor because she cannot blink on command. On the 2025 judgment, the bank's position is

options.A: tenable, because authentication standards are a matter of policy discretion which the Court left untouched in its directions to regulators
options.B: untenable, as the liveness check must have alternatives
options.C: untenable only if the survivor can show that she has first made a written complaint to the Reserve Bank of India's ombudsman
options.D: tenable, because digital access protects only persons with visual impairment and does not extend to facial disfigurement of any degree

questions.explanation: The Court directed alternatives to the blinking check and described bridging the digital divide as a constitutional imperative, not policy discretion.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the quoted holding. Option D wrongly limits the petitioners' categories. Option C invents an exhaustion-of-remedies requirement.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options use real vocabulary (policy discretion, ombudsman) to sound cautious.
questions.language_trick: 'untenable' is a legal conclusion; the reason is in the second half of the sentence.

questions.question: Under Mission Accessibility, UPSC's notification must allow a candidate eligible for a scribe to seek a change of scribe

options.A: at any time before entering the examination hall, because the right to a scribe is absolute under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act
options.B: once only in an examination cycle, and not later than thirty days before the examination
options.C: up to at least seven days before the date of the examination, as the notification must permit such a change
options.D: only within seven days after the declaration of the preliminary result

questions.explanation: The Court's words are 'up to at least seven days prior' to the examination.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D shifts the timeline to after a result. Option A says 'absolute', which the order does not. Option B adds a once-only rule and a thirty-day limit.
questions.clat_trap: A numerical detail drawn from the quotation; two wrong options use larger numbers or absolutes.
questions.language_trick: 'at least' sets a minimum period, not a maximum.

questions.question: The Court's statement that a public body must 'move beyond formal equality to ensure substantive inclusion' reflects the idea that

options.A: reservation in public employment is the only constitutionally acceptable means of achieving substantive equality for disabled persons in public services
options.B: substantive equality is a directive principle and therefore cannot be enforced against a statutory body such as UPSC
options.C: equality means identical treatment of all candidates, so exceptions for disabled candidates are tolerated only as acts of administrative benevolence
options.D: treating unequally placed persons identically can entrench disadvantage, so differential measures are needed to realise equality in practice

questions.explanation: Substantive equality looks to outcomes and accommodation. The decision is reported as treating rights of persons with disabilities as constitutional promises, not benevolence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C states formal equality, the reading the Court moves beyond. Option A narrows substantive equality to reservation. Option B wrongly treats equality as a non-justiciable principle.
questions.clat_trap: 'formal' versus 'substantive' is the central contrast; the first wrong option restates 'formal'.
questions.language_trick: 'beyond' signals that formal equality is insufficient.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The right to digital access recognised in Pragya Prasun/Amar Jain can be claimed only by persons with disabilities. Reason (R): The Court described bridging the digital divide as a constitutional imperative and not a matter of policy discretion.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The petitions arose from disability, but the Court's statement is general: digital access is part of the right to life and liberty. A is therefore false, while R reproduces the Court's words.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A restricts a general right to the petitioners' class. R is accurate.
questions.clat_trap: The facts of the petition tempt the reader to confine the principle to the petitioners' class.
questions.language_trick: 'can be claimed only by' is an absolute limit that the quoted holding does not impose.

passages.subject_area: Constitutional Law and Education Law (Mental Health, Article 21)
passages.title: Student Mental Health: Sukdeb Saha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2025) and Amit Kumar v. Union of India (2026)
passages.passage: Parliament enacted the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, which gives every person a right to access mental healthcare and presumes that a person who attempts suicide is under severe stress. Yet it took two judgments to bring the subject into the classroom. In Sukdeb Saha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2025 INSC 893, 25 July 2025), Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta JJ., with Mehta J. writing, considered the death of a seventeen-year-old NEET aspirant from West Bengal, who fell from the third floor of a hostel in Visakhapatnam in July 2023. The Andhra Pradesh High Court had refused a CBI inquiry on 14 February 2024. The Supreme Court reversed that order, observing that “the power to transfer an investigation to the CBI is not to be exercised as a matter of course”, but finding the local investigation ineffective. It then declared: “Mental health is an integral component of the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.” Acting under Article 32, it issued fifteen guidelines, including a mental-health policy for institutions, a trained counsellor in every institution with 100 or more students, curbs on ranking-based segregation in coaching centres, and safeguards in residential premises. They “shall remain in force and be binding until such time as appropriate legislation or regulatory frameworks are enacted by the competent authority.” The technique recalls Vishaka (1997), where guidelines filled a legislative vacuum. In Amit Kumar v. Union of India (2026 INSC 62, 15 January 2026), Pardiwala and Mahadevan JJ. went further, relying on a National Task Force and using Article 142. The Court noted that “the purely quantitative expansion without any adequate institutional support framework, has left students vulnerable” and that “cases are suppressed and proceedings are often biased.” It directed that “all HEIs must report any incident of suicide or unnatural death of a student”, required annual reports to the UGC and professional regulators, asked for qualified medical help round the clock on residential campuses or within a kilometre, set four months to fill vacancies and clear scholarship arrears, and asked the Task Force to prepare a model suicide prevention and postvention protocol. The Amit Kumar quotations are as reproduced in a law-report summary; check them against the order text.
verbatim_extracts: the power to transfer an investigation to the CBI is not to be exercised as a matter of course
Mental health is an integral component of the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution of India
shall remain in force and be binding until such time as appropriate legislation or regulatory frameworks are enacted by the competent authority
The purely quantitative expansion without any adequate institutional support framework, has left students vulnerable
Cases are suppressed and proceedings are often biased
All HEIs must report any incident of suicide or unnatural death of a student

questions.question: The guidelines in Sukdeb Saha are expressed to remain in force 'until such time as appropriate legislation or regulatory frameworks are enacted'. This technique is closest to

options.A: Vishaka (1997), where the Court laid down binding guidelines to fill a legislative vacuum until Parliament enacted a law
options.B: an interim order under Article 136 that lapses automatically when the special leave petition is disposed of
options.C: a declaration under Article 13 that existing laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void to the extent of the inconsistency
options.D: an advisory opinion under Article 143, which binds only the President who sought it and creates no rule for private institutions

questions.explanation: Both Vishaka and Sukdeb Saha used constitutional jurisdiction to issue guidelines that bind until legislation occupies the field.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D misdescribes the nature of advisory opinions. Option B treats the guidelines as a mere interim order. Option C confuses a vacuum-filling exercise with striking down existing laws.
questions.clat_trap: The idea of binding guidelines pending law is familiar, but each wrong option names a different, real constitutional device.
questions.language_trick: 'until such time as' marks a temporary but binding regime.

questions.question: A coaching institute in Kota with 120 students has no counsellor. After Sukdeb Saha, the institute

options.A: is in breach only if a student has already died, since the guidelines operate as a response to a completed unnatural death on its premises
options.B: is in breach, as institutions of 100 or more students must engage a trained counsellor, psychologist or social worker
options.C: is not in breach, because the counsellor requirement applies only to government schools and universities and not to private coaching centres of any size
options.D: is not in breach, because the guidelines are non-binding recommendations to State governments until Parliament enacts a statute on the subject

questions.explanation: The guidelines bind until legislation is made and apply to institutions, including coaching centres, with 100 or more students.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C limits the guidelines to public bodies. Option A makes the duty depend on a death. Option D calls binding guidelines mere recommendations.
questions.clat_trap: The threshold of 100 students is a detail that decides the hypothetical.
questions.language_trick: '100 or more' includes 120.

questions.question: What best explains the Court's decision on the CBI transfer in Sukdeb Saha?

options.A: The family alleged suicide and a central agency becomes mandatory whenever a death occurs in a hostel recommended by an institute
options.B: Every unnatural death of a student must be investigated by the CBI under the guidelines, so the transfer followed as of right
options.C: Transfer is exceptional and not a matter of course, but here the local investigation was found ineffective because of an unexplained suicide narrative, CCTV inconsistencies, conflicting medical records and lost forensic material
options.D: The High Court had no power to order a CBI inquiry where First Information Reports were registered in more than one State of the Union

questions.explanation: The Court recited the caution against routine transfers and then gave case-specific reasons for transfer.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D invents a jurisdictional bar. Option B treats the guidelines as imposing CBI inquiry. Option A inverts the family's allegation and invents a mandatory rule.
questions.clat_trap: The opening words of the correct option echo the quotation 'not to be exercised as a matter of course', yet the Court still ordered transfer. Students may reject the right option for that reason.
questions.language_trick: 'but here' joins rule to exception.

questions.question: Which direction was issued in Amit Kumar, as described in the passage?

options.A: Vacancies of teaching and non-teaching staff must be filled within twelve months, and scholarship arrears cleared within two years
options.B: Private HEIs, but not Central institutions, must file annual reports of student suicides with the UGC and the professional regulators
options.C: School and higher education student suicides must be recorded together in one NCRB category so that comparison is not possible
options.D: Residential HEIs must secure round-the-clock qualified medical help on campus or within a kilometre

questions.explanation: The passage records round-the-clock medical help on residential campuses or within a kilometre.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B limits reporting to private HEIs. Option A replaces four months with twelve months and two years. Option C reverses the direction to distinguish categories.
questions.clat_trap: The wrong options alter a number, a class or a direction; read each against the passage.
questions.language_trick: 'within a kilometre' is the detail in the passage.

questions.question: The Court's criticism that 'purely quantitative expansion without any adequate institutional support framework' has left students vulnerable suggests that

options.A: expansion of seats in higher education violates Article 21A and must therefore be curtailed
options.B: student suicides are caused chiefly by examination rankings, which the Court directed be abolished
options.C: private institutions alone have expanded, while the State's own institutions have maintained adequate support structures throughout
options.D: growth in enrolment and institutions was not matched by support structures for the students admitted to them

questions.explanation: The Court's concern is the absence of support alongside growth, not growth itself.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns criticism of unsupported growth into a bar on growth. Option C limits the criticism to private institutions. Option B invents a causal finding and an abolition direction.
questions.clat_trap: 'quantitative' contrasts with 'institutional support'; the first wrong option reads it as a ban.
questions.language_trick: 'purely' qualifies the criticism.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements.
I. Sukdeb Saha held mental health to be an integral component of the right to life under Article 21.
II. The guidelines issued in Sukdeb Saha are mere recommendations to the States and have no binding force.
III. In Amit Kumar the Court invoked Article 142 and relied on a National Task Force.
IV. Amit Kumar held that HEIs need not report a student's unnatural death to the police.
Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and III are correct. Statement II is false because the guidelines are binding until legislation is enacted, and statement IV is false because HEIs must report.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: 'I only' omits III. 'II and IV only' selects the two false statements. 'I, III and IV only' includes the false IV.
questions.clat_trap: Statements II and IV contradict the quoted language, but a student who recalls only 'guidelines' may accept II.
questions.language_trick: 'mere recommendations' versus 'binding until legislation'.

passages.subject_area: Constitutional Law and Animal Welfare Law (Article 21 and Public Safety)
passages.title: Stray Dogs, Institutional Spaces and Article 21: In Re: City Hounded by Strays, Kids Pay the Price (2025-2026)
passages.passage: Few judicial proceedings of 2025 aroused as much public argument as the suo motu case on stray dogs. It began when the Supreme Court took notice of reports of dog bites and rabies deaths, especially of children. After an order of 22 August 2025 had modified an earlier approach for the National Capital Region by allowing re-release of dogs, an order of 7 November 2025 extended directions to institutional areas such as schools, hospitals, sports complexes, bus stands and depots, and railway stations, calling for removal of stray dogs from those premises and a bar on their re-release there. Applications sought recall, clarification or expansion. On 19 May 2026, a bench of Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and N.V. Anjaria JJ., with Mehta J. writing, disposed of the questions. Two provisions of the Animal Birth Control (Dogs) Rules, 2023 were central. Rule 7(2) speaks of dogs in a “gated campus”, and Rule 11(19) permits sterilised and vaccinated dogs to be returned to the “same place or locality”. The Court said that “the provisions must be interpreted in a purposive and contextual manner”, read “gated campus” narrowly so that it does not cover sensitive institutional premises, and confined “same place or locality” to publicly accessible open spaces. On Article 142 it said that “public policy, properly understood, must operate in furtherance of constitutional values”, and it observed that “the absence of a conventional lis does not dilute the judicial function.” On Article 21 it declared: “The right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India stands at the highest pedestal of constitutional protection”, a sentence that goes on to describe the State's duty. The final directions required at least one working ABC centre in each district, stocks of anti-rabies vaccine and immunoglobulin, a time-bound mechanism for stray cattle on national highways, protection from criminal proceedings for officials acting in good faith, and permitted euthanasia of rabid, incurably ill or demonstrably dangerous dogs after prior assessment by qualified veterinary experts under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 and the 2023 Rules. Monitoring passed to High Courts, and the matter is listed on 17 November 2026. The background is Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja (2014), which read Article 21 and the duty of compassion in Article 51A(g) generously in favour of animals. Verify later orders.
verbatim_extracts: The provisions must be interpreted in a purposive and contextual manner
Public policy, properly understood, must operate in furtherance of constitutional values
The absence of a conventional lis does not dilute the judicial function
The right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India stands at the highest pedestal of constitutional protection

questions.question: In which provision did the Court read the phrase 'gated campus' narrowly?

options.A: Rule 7(2) of the ABC Rules, 2023
options.B: Section 11 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, which regulates the treatment of animals by those who have charge of them
options.C: Article 51A(g) of the Constitution, whose reference to compassion for living creatures forms part of the fundamental duties
options.D: Rule 11(19) of the ABC Rules, 2023, which governs the return of sterilised and vaccinated dogs to the same place or locality

questions.explanation: The passage places 'gated campus' in Rule 7(2) and says it was read narrowly. Rule 11(19) concerns 'same place or locality'.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D is the neighbouring rule with a different phrase. Option B and Option C are authorities cited as background but not the source of the phrase.
questions.clat_trap: The two Rules are adjacent and each has its own quoted phrase; matching phrase to provision is the test.
questions.language_trick: Quoted phrases are tied to specific provisions.

questions.question: On the Court's treatment of Article 142 in this matter,

options.A: Article 142 cannot be used at all in suo motu proceedings, because there is no conventional lis between the contending parties who appear before the Court
options.B: Article 142 was not invoked, as the directions rest wholly on the ABC Rules, 2023 and require no additional constitutional source
options.C: Article 142 is bounded by public policy, and no public policy principle supports the continued presence of strays in sensitive institutional areas
options.D: Article 142 lets the Court override statutory rules wherever it considers it just, without any limit of public policy or any constitutional values whatsoever

questions.explanation: The Court said public policy must operate in furtherance of constitutional values and that the absence of a conventional lis does not dilute the judicial function.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the lis remark. Option D removes the public-policy limit. Option B denies the Article 142 discussion.
questions.clat_trap: Three options are statements about Article 142 that sound plausible in isolation; only one fits both quotations.
questions.language_trick: 'bounded' and 'no ... support' are the key words.

questions.question: The relationship between the 19 May 2026 judgment and the November 2025 order is that

options.A: the judgment overruled the November order and permitted re-release of sterilised dogs in every location, institutional or otherwise, once they are vaccinated
options.B: the judgment replaced the November order with a nationwide prohibition on stray dogs in all public places, without exception
options.C: the judgment referred the validity of the November order to a larger bench and stayed its operation till that bench decides
options.D: the judgment reaffirmed the November directions insofar as they exclude institutional premises from re-release, and earlier orders remained in force

questions.explanation: The passage says the Court reaffirmed the November directions regarding institutional premises, and that earlier orders remain in force.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the opposite. Option B overstates the scope. Option C invents a reference and a stay.
questions.clat_trap: A later judgment on 'applications for recall' can be mistaken for a recall.
questions.language_trick: 'reaffirmed' and 'insofar as' narrow the scope.

questions.question: Which condition applies to euthanasia of dogs under the directions?

options.A: It is permitted only for rabid, incurably ill or demonstrably dangerous dogs after prior veterinary assessment and in accordance with the 1960 Act and the 2023 Rules
options.B: It is permitted for all unsterilised dogs found in institutional premises after thirty days' notice to the nearest animal welfare organisation and the local body concerned
options.C: It is never permitted, since the Court held that Article 21 also protects the life of animals against killing in every circumstance
options.D: It is permitted for any stray dog in an area with frequent bites, on the order of the local officer without any veterinary assessment

questions.explanation: The directions allow euthanasia only for specified categories of dogs, after assessment by qualified veterinary experts.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D removes the assessment requirement. Option B invents a category and a notice period. Option C states an absolute prohibition that the Court did not adopt.
questions.clat_trap: Absolute words in the third option mirror Nagaraja's expansive Article 21, but the Court held otherwise.
questions.language_trick: 'only' and 'prior' narrow the power.

questions.question: An officer, acting in good faith under the Court's directions, removes strays from a hospital campus. An activist files an FIR for cruelty. On the judgment, the FIR

options.A: can proceed as a matter of course, because the protection extends only to the Animal Welfare Board and not to local officials
options.B: can proceed only if the activist first obtains the High Court's sanction
options.C: must be quashed in every case, because officials acting under judicial directions enjoy absolute immunity from criminal liability
options.D: cannot proceed against the officer unless mala fides or clear abuse of power is shown

questions.explanation: The directions protect officials acting in good faith from FIRs and criminal proceedings unless mala fides or clear abuse is shown.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confines the protection to the Board. Option C turns it into absolute immunity. Option B invents a sanction.
questions.clat_trap: Absolute immunity is an overstatement; the protection is conditional.
questions.language_trick: 'unless' sets the exception.

questions.question: Assertion (A): In reading the ABC Rules, 2023, the Court restricted the re-release of stray dogs in sensitive institutional premises. Reason (R): The Court held that the Rules give stray dogs an unqualified right to remain in every location.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Court read the Rules purposively and said they do not give stray dogs an unqualified right to remain in every location. A is true and R is false.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R states the opposite of the Court's reading.
questions.clat_trap: A true statement is paired with a reversed reason that echoes 'rights' language familiar from Nagaraja.
questions.language_trick: 'unqualified' and 'every' are absolutes the Court rejected.

passages.title: Menstrual Health as Part of Article 21 and Article 21A: Dr Jaya Thakur v. Government of India (2026)
passages.passage: In Dr Jaya Thakur v. Government of India (2026 INSC 97), a bench of J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan JJ. decided a public interest petition, filed in 2022, on the absence of menstrual hygiene facilities for schoolgirls. The judgment is reported to have been delivered on 30 January 2026 (verify the date). The Court did not treat the matter as one of charity or mere administration. It held that menstrual health falls within the right to life and dignity under Article 21, and that the right to free education under Article 21A is hollow if a girl cannot attend school during her period. The Court said: “menstrual hygiene management is not confined to sanitation, it includes bodily autonomy and decisional freedom.” It insisted that the school environment, and not only its infrastructure, must be free of stigma, and held that boys too must be educated: “Menstruation should not be a topic that is only shared in hushed whispers.” The history matters. Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) and Unni Krishnan v. State of A.P. (1993) read a right to education up to the age of fourteen into Article 21, long before the Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 later fixed norms in its Schedule, including separate toilets for boys and girls. As summarised in secondary reports, the Court treated those norms as part of the content of Article 21A, so that non-compliance by a school is a constitutional, and not merely an administrative, default. The reported directions apply to government-run and privately managed schools alike: functional gender-segregated toilets with water, free sanitary napkins, menstrual hygiene management corners, safe disposal, sensitisation of male and female teachers, gender-responsive curricula through NCERT and SCERT, and periodic inspection by District Education Officers (verify against the judgment).
verbatim_extracts: menstrual hygiene management is not confined to sanitation, it includes bodily autonomy and decisional freedom.
Menstruation should not be a topic that is only shared in hushed whispers.

questions.question: The Court observed that menstrual hygiene management “is not confined to sanitation.” This observation most directly supports the view that

options.A: the claim engages a girl's bodily autonomy and decisional freedom, so the duty is wider than facilities
options.B: the State's duty ends once every school has a separate toilet and a stock of napkins, because nothing more is needed
options.C: the question is one of health policy alone and therefore lies outside judicial enforcement by directions
options.D: the right is traceable only to Article 15(3), which allows special provision for women and children

questions.explanation: The Court tied menstrual hygiene to bodily autonomy and decisional freedom, which are facets of dignity under Article 21. The duty therefore reaches beyond the supply of toilets and napkins.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B confines the duty to infrastructure, which is exactly what the quoted words reject. Option D drops Article 21 and treats Article 15(3) as the sole source. Option C treats the subject as non-justiciable, although the Court issued enforceable directions.
questions.clat_trap: Option Option B sounds practical and tempts a reader who ignores the word 'not confined'.
questions.language_trick: 'is not confined to' signals that the concept is wider than the thing named; the answer must be the one that widens the duty.

questions.question: According to the passage, the link between the 2009 Act's Schedule norms and Article 21A is that the Court treated the norms as

options.A: a replacement for Article 21A, which the Court held to have been superseded by the Act of 2009 on this subject
options.B: a set of aspirational standards that the State may relax for privately managed schools on grounds of cost
options.C: part of the content of the Article 21A guarantee, so that a school's failure to meet them, including the requirement of separate toilets for boys and girls, is a constitutional default and not an administrative lapse
options.D: a statutory matter alone, enforceable only through the grievance machinery created by the Act and not under Article 32

questions.explanation: The passage says the Court treated the Schedule's norms as part of the content of Article 21A, so non-compliance is a constitutional default.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B contradicts the reported direction that private schools are covered. Option D separates the statute from the Constitution, which the Court refused to do. Option A reverses the relationship, since the Act gives effect to Article 21A.
questions.clat_trap: A student who assumes that a statute cannot raise a constitutional breach will choose the 'statutory matter alone' option.
questions.language_trick: 'is part of the content of' versus 'a replacement for': the preposition decides who is subordinate to whom.

questions.question: A private unaided school argues that the directions bind only government schools because it receives no State aid. On the passage, this argument is

options.A: sustainable, because Article 21A imposes its obligation only on the State and its aided institutions, and an unaided school is a private body
options.B: unsustainable only for those private schools that admit pupils under the quota reserved for economically weaker sections
options.C: sustainable in part, since only the requirement of free sanitary napkins is imposed on private schools and the other directions are optional
