options.D: unsustainable, as the directions extend to private schools too

questions.explanation: The reported directions apply to government-run and privately managed schools alike, so the argument fails.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A assumes a limit that the directions do not recognise. Option C invents a partial application. Option B adds a quota-based condition that appears nowhere in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The aid-based distinction feels natural from older education cases, but the passage extends the directions to all schools.
questions.language_trick: 'alike' in the passage is the decisive word; options with 'only' import restrictions.

questions.question: Which statement about the constitutional history behind the judgment is accurate on the passage?

options.A: Unni Krishnan (1993) held that the right to education arises under Article 21A, which already existed then
options.B: Article 21A followed the case law that read education into Article 21
options.C: The Right to Education Act, 2009 preceded Mohini Jain and Unni Krishnan, which interpreted that Act
options.D: Article 21A was inserted by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act and was relied on in Mohini Jain (1992)

questions.explanation: Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993) read the right to education into Article 21; Article 21A came later through the Eighty-sixth Amendment in 2002, and the 2009 Act followed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D gives the wrong amendment and the wrong order. Option A anachronistically places Article 21A before 1993. Option C reverses the sequence of the Act and the cases.
questions.clat_trap: Chronology questions are traps because every option names the same cases but shuffles their dates.
questions.language_trick: Look at 'followed' and 'preceded': the sequence word is the whole question.

questions.question: The direction that boys, and male teachers, be educated and sensitised proceeds on the premise that

options.A: physical facilities are secondary and the real remedy lies in changing the curriculum alone
options.B: the stigma in schools is attributable to male students and is not shared by female students or staff at all
options.C: menstruation is a subject on which only girls and women teachers have the competence to counsel schoolchildren effectively
options.D: stigma among peers and staff can keep a girl out of school even where the facilities are adequate

questions.explanation: The Court insisted that the whole school environment be free of stigma; an unsensitised male student may harass a menstruating girl and keep her away from school.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C contradicts the direction that male teachers be sensitised. Option A dismisses facilities, whereas the Court required both. Option B blames only boys and ignores peers and staff generally.
questions.clat_trap: Option Option A looks progressive but sets facilities and curriculum against each other, which the passage does not do.
questions.language_trick: 'even where' in the correct option connects to 'A school may have adequate facilities' in the reported reasoning.

questions.question: Consider the following statements about the judgment as presented in the passage. I. Menstrual health was held to fall within Article 21. II. The reported directions are confined to government-run schools. III. The Schedule norms of the 2009 Act were treated as part of Article 21A. IV. Article 21A was inserted by the judgment itself.

options.A: I and III only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and III restate the passage. II is wrong because private schools are covered. IV is wrong because Article 21A was inserted by the Eighty-sixth Amendment in 2002.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement II fails on 'alike'. Statement IV confuses a judicial reading with a constitutional amendment.
questions.clat_trap: The statement-combination format rewards eliminating II and IV; a student who accepts IV because the judgment 'created' a right will go wrong.
questions.language_trick: 'inserted' is the language of amendment; courts interpret, they do not insert articles.

passages.title: Caste Discrimination on Campus and Interim Judicial Review: Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India (2026)
passages.passage: On 29 January 2026, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Joymalya Bagchi J., in Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India (2026 SCC OnLine SC 134), kept in abeyance the University Grants Commission (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulations, 2026. Exercising Article 142, the Court directed that the 2012 Regulations “will continue to operate and remain in force till further orders.” The petitioners, who included general-category students, attacked the definition of “caste-based discrimination” in Regulation 3(1)(c) as restrictive, arguing that it left persons outside the reserved categories without a remedy and assumed that discrimination travels in one direction. The Court's reasoning was prima facie and interim: “some of the provisions of the Impugned Regulations suffer from certain ambiguities” and “the possibility of their misuse cannot be ruled out.” It framed the question whether the clause “bears a reasonable and rational nexus to subserve the object and purpose” of the Regulations, and, as reported, directed that the connected petitions be heard by a three-judge bench. In an oral remark the bench asked whether the country was “going backwards from whatever we gained in terms of achieving a casteless society.” On 20 August 2026 the Solicitor General told the Court that the regulations were “under reconsideration,” and the UGC was asked to file a counter affidavit within four weeks. The stay appears to continue (verify current status). The history explains the stakes. The regulations were driven by the deaths of Rohith Vemula (Hyderabad, 2016) and Payal Tadvi (Mumbai, 2019), whose mothers petitioned the Supreme Court in 2019 for effective rules against caste discrimination in campuses. Constitutionally the field is anchored in Articles 15(1), 17 and 46, and in the premise of Article 14 that a classification must bear a rational nexus to its object.
verbatim_extracts: will continue to operate and remain in force till further orders.
some of the provisions of the Impugned Regulations suffer from certain ambiguities
the possibility of their misuse cannot be ruled out.
bears a reasonable and rational nexus to subserve the object and purpose
going backwards from whatever we gained in terms of achieving a casteless society

questions.question: The order of 29 January 2026 is best described as

options.A: an approval of the 2026 Regulations, coupled with a suggestion that the definition of caste-based discrimination be widened later
options.B: a final declaration that Regulation 3(1)(c) is void as it violates Article 14, with the rest of the Regulations saved by severance
options.C: a direction to the UGC to withdraw the 2026 Regulations and to frame fresh ones within a period fixed by the bench
options.D: an interim measure resting on a prima facie view, with the merits left for later decision

questions.explanation: The Court spoke of ambiguities and the possibility of misuse and framed a question for hearing by a larger bench; it did not decide the validity of the clause.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B converts an interim stay into a final holding. Option C invents a direction to withdraw. Option A reverses the order, since the Regulations were kept in abeyance.
questions.clat_trap: 'Held in abeyance' feels like 'struck down', which tempts the reader to choose the final-declaration option.
questions.language_trick: 'prima facie' and 'interim' are the marks of non-final relief.

questions.question: The Court's use of Article 142 to continue the 2012 Regulations shows that it

options.A: held that the UGC Act, 1956 does not authorise the framing of any equity regulations after 2012
options.B: exercised a power to amend regulations made by the UGC, since Article 142 permits the Court to legislate
options.C: sought to avoid a regulatory gap on campus discrimination while the 2026 text was under challenge before the Court
options.D: accepted that the 2012 Regulations are the better statement of the law and held them valid as a final matter on the merits

questions.explanation: Article 142 allows complete justice in the case; here it prevented a vacuum by reviving the earlier framework 'till further orders'. It neither validated the 2012 text finally nor legislated.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D turns an interim revival into a final holding. Option B claims a power to amend the regulations, which the Court did not exercise. Option A invents a holding on the UGC's competence.
questions.clat_trap: Article 142 is often mistaken for a general law-making power, which makes the 'amend' option attractive.
questions.language_trick: 'till further orders' in the quotation limits the revival in time.

questions.question: The question whether Regulation 3(1)(c) “bears a reasonable and rational nexus” to the object of the Regulations is drawn from which constitutional test?

options.A: The test of essential religious practice under Article 25, which asks whether a practice is integral to the religion
options.B: The test of reasonable restriction under Article 19(2), which requires that a restriction be in the interest of public order
options.C: The test of basic structure review under Article 368, which asks whether an amendment alters the framework of the Constitution
options.D: The classification test under Article 14, which requires an intelligible differentia and a rational nexus with the object

questions.explanation: The wording 'reasonable and rational nexus' is the second limb of the Article 14 classification test, as the passage notes.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B belongs to Article 19. Option A belongs to the law on religion. Option C concerns constitutional amendments, not regulations.
questions.clat_trap: All options use a familiar constitutional test; only the phrase 'rational nexus' identifies Article 14.
questions.language_trick: 'nexus' is the key word and points to classification.

questions.question: Which fact, according to the passage, forms part of the background to the 2026 Regulations?

options.A: A Constitution Bench ruling in Indra Sawhney (1992) directing the UGC to frame anti-ragging regulations
options.B: The petition of the mothers of Rohith Vemula and Payal Tadvi in the Supreme Court
options.C: An amendment of Article 15 in 2019 requiring universities to publish caste-wise admission data
options.D: A report of the Sachar Committee recommending reservation in universities for minority communities

questions.explanation: The passage records that the deaths of Rohith Vemula and Payal Tadvi, whose mothers petitioned the Court in 2019, drove the regulations.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D brings in an unrelated committee. Option A invents a direction in Indra Sawhney. Option C invents an amendment.
questions.clat_trap: Familiar names and years from other topics create plausible but false 'background' options.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A general-category student alleges harassment on caste grounds by a classmate in a university, in March 2026. On the passage, the regulations that continue to operate are

options.A: the 2012 Regulations alone, as directed to remain in force till further orders while the 2026 Regulations are held in abeyance
options.B: both the 2012 and 2026 Regulations, which operate together until the three-judge bench decides
options.C: the 2026 Regulations in full, because the stay applies only to Regulation 3(1)(c) and the remaining clauses of the 2026 text are in force
options.D: neither set, as the Court's order left the field to the criminal law and to the universities' own policies

questions.explanation: The 2026 Regulations were kept in abeyance and the 2012 Regulations remained in force, so the later set cannot be invoked.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C misreads the abeyance as limited to one clause. Option B invents concurrent operation. Option D suggests a vacuum, which Article 142 was used to avoid.
questions.clat_trap: Many readers recall the challenge to clause 3(c) and assume the stay is limited to that clause.
questions.language_trick: 'kept in abeyance' applies to the Regulations as a whole.

questions.question: Assertion (A): By its order of 29 January 2026 the Supreme Court struck down Regulation 3(1)(c) of the 2026 Regulations. Reason (R): The Court observed that the possibility of misuse of the Regulations cannot be ruled out.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because the order was an interim stay and not a decision on validity. R is true, being a quoted observation.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: The observation in R is a ground for interim caution, not for a final holding.
questions.clat_trap: Because R is a true quotation, students accept that it must explain A, forgetting that A is itself false.
questions.language_trick: 'struck down' versus 'kept in abeyance'.

passages.title: Betting on Skill: State of Tamil Nadu v. Junglee Games India Pvt. Ltd. (2026)
passages.passage: In State of Tamil Nadu v. Junglee Games India Pvt. Ltd. (2026 INSC 594), a bench of J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan JJ. reversed the Madras and Karnataka High Courts, which had struck down State laws prohibiting online rummy and poker played for stakes. The report is dated 27 May 2026 (verify). The High Courts had read “betting and gambling” in Entry 34 of the State List as limited to games of chance, so that betting on games of skill fell outside State competence. The Supreme Court disagreed: “The protection afforded to games of skill under Entry 34 cannot be construed as protection to betting on games of skill.” It added that “Both betting and gambling involve the aspect of staking money on an uncertainty,” and described the contrary High Court reading as “a clear Constitutional aberration, tinkering with the Constitution or actually rewriting the Constitutional text.” Once money is staked, the character of the game stops being relevant. Betting and gambling are res extra commercium and therefore lie outside Article 19(1)(g), so the proportionality test does not arise. The Court also found that online money gaming has a proximate nexus with public tranquillity, so a State may rely on Entry 1 (public order) as well, and noted that the Tamil Nadu law rested on empirical data from the Justice K. Chandru Committee. The history is important. State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala (1957) held that gambling is not 'trade' under Article 19(1)(g), and K.R. Lakshmanan v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996) treated horse racing as a game of skill. The Court said Chamarbaugwala never decided whether 'betting' differs from 'gambling' in Entry 34, and that Lakshmanan merely interpreted a legislative exception for horse racing. The Online Gaming Act, 2025, a central law facing its own challenge, was not decided here (verify current status).
verbatim_extracts: The protection afforded to games of skill under Entry 34 cannot be construed as protection to betting on games of skill
Both betting and gambling involve the aspect of staking money on an uncertainty
a clear Constitutional aberration, tinkering with the Constitution or actually rewriting the Constitutional text

questions.question: A State enacts a law that prohibits online card games played for money stakes, but leaves untouched the same games played without stakes. On the passage, the law is

options.A: valid only if the State first proves, on the evidence of each game, that the game is predominantly one of chance rather than skill
options.B: beyond State competence, as Entry 34 protects every game of skill from State regulation and permits the State to regulate only games of chance
options.C: within State competence under Entry 34, because the immunity of skill games does not reach betting on them, so the stakes-based line is valid whatever the game's character
options.D: valid only if Parliament has not occupied the field, since betting on games of skill falls within a central entry and not within Entry 34

questions.explanation: The Court held that once stakes are introduced the nature of the game is not decisive, and Entry 34 empowers a State to prohibit betting on games of skill.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B repeats the High Court view that the Court called a constitutional aberration. Option A makes skill versus chance decisive, which the Court rejected. Option D invents a central entry.
questions.clat_trap: Students who remember Chamarbaugwala or Lakshmanan may assume that skill games are always protected.
questions.language_trick: 'for stakes' is the operative phrase; the line is drawn at money staked.

questions.question: The Court's statement that betting and gambling are res extra commercium implies that

options.A: the activity may be prohibited only if it is conducted online and not if conducted physically
options.B: the State must justify the prohibition by showing that it is a reasonable restriction under Article 19(6) of the Constitution
options.C: the activity is protected under Article 19(1)(g) but the State may restrict it in the interest of public order
options.D: no proportionality inquiry arises under Article 19(1)(g), as the activity is outside the protected trade

questions.explanation: If an activity is outside the freedom of trade, Article 19(6) and proportionality are not reached. The passage says exactly this.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B assumes the activity is within Article 19(1)(g). Option C makes the same mistake. Option A brings in a distinction between online and offline that the passage does not make.
questions.clat_trap: Option Option B is the standard framework for any trade, which is why it feels safe.
questions.language_trick: 'res extra commercium' means 'outside commerce', so the restriction analysis never starts.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the Court's treatment of State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala (1957)?

options.A: It was applied as authority that games of skill are always outside the competence of the State legislature
options.B: It was distinguished since online games did not exist in 1957
options.C: It was overruled, because it had wrongly held that gambling is not trade under Article 19(1)(g)
options.D: It was held not to have decided whether betting differs from gambling in Entry 34

questions.explanation: The Court said the earlier case did not address the question of betting versus gambling in Entry 34, and so did not restrict the States.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C says the case was overruled, but the passage uses it for the proposition on Article 19(1)(g). Option A reverses its effect. Option B gives a reason that the passage does not state.
questions.clat_trap: Students often assume a new judgment must overrule an old one.
questions.language_trick: 'did not decide' is not 'overruled'.

questions.question: Which statement is consistent with the Court's treatment of K.R. Lakshmanan v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996)?

options.A: It held that betting on all games of skill is a fundamental right, which the State may restrict only by a reasonable law
options.B: It interpreted a legislative exception for horse racing in the Tamil Nadu law and did not limit State power over betting on games of skill
options.C: It struck down the Tamil Nadu law on racing, because racing was held to involve no element of gambling at all
options.D: It was relied on to show that a State may not legislate on betting without prior approval of Parliament

questions.explanation: The Court read Lakshmanan as concerned with the horse-racing exception that the legislature had itself created, so it does not constrain State power over betting.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns a statutory exception into a fundamental right. Option C reverses the outcome of the case and the reasoning. Option D invents a requirement of approval.
questions.clat_trap: The words 'game of skill' in Lakshmanan invite over-reading.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The Court's reliance on the Justice K. Chandru Committee's empirical data serves chiefly to show that

options.A: the State had a factual basis, drawn from the Committee's findings, to link online money gaming with public order
options.B: the High Courts had lacked the power to look at empirical material in a constitutional challenge to a State enactment
options.C: the committee's recommendation was binding on the Court under Article 141
options.D: Parliament had delegated its power on betting to the State through the committee's report

questions.explanation: The data supported the finding of a proximate nexus between online money gaming and public tranquillity, which allowed reliance on Entry 1.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D invents a delegation. Option C treats a committee report as a binding precedent. Option B invents a limit on the High Courts' powers.
questions.clat_trap: Committee reports often appear in these judgments, and students wrongly credit them with binding force.
questions.language_trick: 'binding' versus 'supporting': a report supports a finding but does not bind.

questions.question: Consider the following statements on the judgment. I. The Court held that betting and gambling fall outside Article 19(1)(g). II. The Court held that Entry 34 protects betting on games of skill. III. The Court found that online money gaming has a proximate nexus with public tranquillity. IV. The Court struck down the Online Gaming Act, 2025.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: III and IV only
options.C: I and III only
options.D: I, II and IV only

questions.explanation: I and III are stated in the passage. II is the reverse of the holding. IV is wrong because the Online Gaming Act, 2025 was not decided in this judgment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement II is the High Court position. Statement IV attributes to the Court a decision on a central law that the passage says was not decided.
questions.clat_trap: The two false statements each use the vocabulary of the correct ones, so a quick reader drifts to the wrong pair.
questions.language_trick: 'protects' versus 'cannot be construed as protection'.

passages.subject_area: Law of Evidence (Electronic Records) and Constitutional Law
passages.title: Hash Value, Expert Certificate and Manifest Arbitrariness: Pune Bar Association v. Union of India (2026)
passages.passage: Pune Bar Association v. Union of India (2026 SCC OnLine SC 1297) was decided on 22 May 2026 by Chief Justice Surya Kant and Joymalya Bagchi and Vipul M. Pancholi JJ. It was a writ petition under Article 32 challenging section 63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which makes a secondary electronic record admissible only with a certificate in the Schedule. Part A is given by the person in charge of the device and discloses the hash value of the record. Part B is given by an expert. The petitioners argued that the requirement was an onerous, technical burden on ordinary litigants and therefore manifestly arbitrary. The Court rejected the challenge. It said: “Hash value of an electronic data is synonymous with an electronic fingerprint,” and held that the requirement “cannot be said to be either arbitrary or unreasonable so as to suffer from the vice of manifest arbitrariness.” The Part B certificate, it added, “provides an additional layer of authenticity to the secondary electronic evidence.” On the signatory of Part B, the Court observed that a person with special skill in computer science and cyber forensics “may sign Part B of the Schedule as an expert” if the Court is satisfied on unimpeachable material, and said the Madras High Court view that only an Examiner of Electronic Evidence notified under section 79A of the Information Technology Act may sign “shall not be treated as a binding precedent.” Yet it also said: “we refrain from giving any conclusive opinion on this issue and keep the question of law open.” The petition was disposed of without issue of notice. Background: section 65B of the Evidence Act, 1872, inserted by the Information Technology Act, 2000, was the predecessor; Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014) and Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020) made its certificate mandatory. Those cases are not cited in this order and are supplied only as history. The ground of manifest arbitrariness in testing legislation was recognised in Shayara Bano (2017).
verbatim_extracts: Hash value of an electronic data is synonymous with an electronic fingerprint
cannot be said to be either arbitrary or unreasonable so as to suffer from the vice of manifest arbitrariness
provides an additional layer of authenticity to the secondary electronic evidence
may sign Part B of the Schedule as an expert
shall not be treated as a binding precedent
we refrain from giving any conclusive opinion on this issue and keep the question of law open

questions.question: In upholding section 63(4), the Court regarded the disclosure of the hash value of an electronic record as

options.A: a technical formality which the Court tolerated though it has no bearing on the authenticity of the record
options.B: a requirement that can be satisfied only by an Examiner of Electronic Evidence notified under section 79A
options.C: a rational means of identifying the record, like a fingerprint, so as to protect the authenticity and integrity of electronic evidence
options.D: an obligation resting on the party opposing the evidence, who must disclose the hash value to the Court

questions.explanation: The Court called the hash value an 'electronic fingerprint' and found a rational nexus with the object of the law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A contradicts the finding of a rational nexus. Option D puts the burden on the opponent, but Part A is given by the person in charge of the device. Option B attributes Part B's expert requirement to Part A.
questions.clat_trap: The three wrong options talk about the same certificate, and the difference lies in who must do what.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The Court's remark that the Madras High Court view “shall not be treated as a binding precedent” is best understood as

options.A: a finding that Part B of the certificate is unconstitutional and must be removed from it
options.B: a direction on the precedential value of that view, without any final decision on who may sign Part B
options.C: a declaration that only a notified Examiner of Electronic Evidence may sign Part B
options.D: an overruling of the Madras High Court judgment by a Constitution Bench with binding force throughout the whole of India

questions.explanation: The Court deprived the High Court view of precedential force but kept the legal question open.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C states the very view the Court refused to treat as binding. Option D wrongly turns an order of a three-judge bench into an overruling by a Constitution Bench. Option A contradicts the holding that the provision is valid.
questions.clat_trap: 'not binding' is different from 'overruled', and the extra bench strength in the wrong option is a bait.
questions.language_trick: 'shall not be treated as' is a precedent-status phrase, not a ruling on merits.

questions.question: The concluding words “keep the question of law open” indicate that

options.A: the scope of expert certification under Part B remains for decision in an appropriate case
options.B: the Union Government has been asked to amend the Schedule so as to settle who may sign Part B within a fixed period
options.C: the challenge to section 63(4) itself remains pending and the section may yet be struck down in this case
options.D: the Court has finally decided that any expert, including a private one, may sign Part B of the certificate, so that no further question can arise

questions.explanation: The Court rejected the challenge to the section but left open who may sign Part B in all cases.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D converts the open question into a final holding. Option C confuses the open question with the validity of the section. Option B invents a direction to the Union.
questions.clat_trap: The Court said 'may' and then added that it gave no conclusive opinion, so a quick reader treats the first part as the holding.
questions.language_trick: 'may sign' in the Court's observation is permissive and is coupled with 'refrain from giving any conclusive opinion'.

questions.question: A litigant relies on this order to argue that only a section 79A Examiner of Electronic Evidence can sign Part B. The best response on the passage is that

options.A: the argument is right, because the Court approved the Madras High Court view and made it binding on every court
options.B: the order does not support the argument, since it declined to treat that view as binding and said that a person with special skill in computer science and cyber forensics may sign Part B as an expert, if the Court is satisfied on unimpeachable material, but left the question open for an appropriate case
options.C: the argument fails because Part B has been removed from the Schedule by the order
options.D: the argument is right, because section 63(4) allows only a notified examiner to certify any secondary electronic record

questions.explanation: The order disapproved of treating the Madras view as binding and allowed a skilled expert to sign, subject to satisfaction of the Court.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A says the opposite of the order. Option D misstates section 63(4), which contemplates an expert, not only a notified examiner. Option C invents the removal of Part B.
questions.clat_trap: The litigant's argument sounds like the Madras High Court's view that the Court expressly refused to endorse.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The passage states that Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer (2014) and Arjun Panditrao (2020) are mentioned as

options.A: authorities relied upon by the Court to uphold section 63(4) of the Adhiniyam
options.B: decisions that held that the certificate is not needed for secondary electronic evidence
options.C: history on the certificate requirement, as the order did not cite them
options.D: precedents that the Court overruled in the order for being inconsistent with the Adhiniyam

questions.explanation: The passage says those cases are not cited in the order and are supplied only as background, since they made the section 65B certificate mandatory.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A says the Court relied on them, but the passage says it did not cite them. Option D invents an overruling. Option B reverses their holding.
questions.clat_trap: The question tests whether the student separates the order's own reasoning from background supplied by the passage-writer.
questions.language_trick: 'only as history' limits the role of those cases.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Supreme Court upheld section 63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 against the challenge of manifest arbitrariness. Reason (R): The Court found that disclosure of the hash value, which is an electronic fingerprint, has a clear and rational nexus with the object of the law.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are correct and R states the reason for the rejection of the challenge.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R gives the ground on which the Court found that the provision was not manifestly arbitrary.
questions.clat_trap: Students may doubt R because the order left the Part B signatory question open, but that question is separate from the validity of the section.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

passages.subject_area: Constitutional Law (Prisoners' Rights) and Criminal Justice
passages.title: Compassionate Release: National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2026)
passages.passage: In National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 162 of 2025), decided on 16 July 2026, a bench of Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta JJ., in a judgment authored by Mehta J., considered the continued imprisonment of convicts and undertrials aged above seventy and of those who are terminally ill, under Articles 14 and 21. The Court opened with the statement that “Prisons, though instruments of lawful confinement, are not spaces where constitutional values are suspended.” It found “a disconnect between normative policy commitments and ground-level execution,” noting that a 2010 Government of India advisory on terminally ill prisoners, itself a sequel to a 2009 Delhi High Court suo motu case, had been unevenly implemented. It also drew on the Law Commission's 268th Report on bail reform and on figures from a NALSA special campaign, which identified 11 terminally ill convicts and 84 convicts above seventy in the States covered (verify the figures). Reasoning that “punishment must not become retributive suffering divorced from proportionality, humanity and purpose,” and that “constitutional restraint cannot be equated with constitutional abdication,” the Court issued directions under Articles 32 and 142. Within three months the Centre, States and Union Territories must notify a policy for early or premature release in consultation with State Legal Services Authorities, using a uniform definition of terminal illness (the UNODC Handbook definition may be adopted); independent Medical Boards at divisional and State levels must certify cases; decisions must be time-bound and reasoned and open to judicial review; Under Trial Review Committees must periodically review eligible prisoners; and the process is to be tracked on the National e-Prisons Portal. Compliance affidavits are due in six months and the matter is listed on 19 January 2027. The history lies in Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1978), which held that prisoners retain their fundamental rights, and in Maneka Gandhi (1978), which required that the procedure affecting life and liberty be just, fair and reasonable.
verbatim_extracts: Prisons, though instruments of lawful confinement, are not spaces where constitutional values are suspended.
punishment must not become retributive suffering divorced from proportionality, humanity and purpose
constitutional restraint cannot be equated with constitutional abdication
a disconnect between normative policy commitments and ground-level execution

questions.question: The statement that “constitutional restraint cannot be equated with constitutional abdication” justifies

options.A: Court directions to compel policy-making after continued executive inaction
options.B: a finding that States have no competence over prisons, which are matters in the Union List
options.C: a view that the Court must wait for Parliament to legislate on compassionate release before issuing any direction
options.D: a rule that the Court may itself decide each prisoner's application for early release under Article 32

questions.explanation: The Court said it was 'duty-bound' to issue directions where inaction persists, but it left the framing of the policy to the Centre and States.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D makes the Court the decision-maker for each prisoner, which the directions do not do. Option B is wrong because prisons are a State subject. Option C is the 'restraint' view the Court rejected.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'restraint' tempts the reader to choose the option that recommends waiting.
questions.language_trick: 'cannot be equated with' marks a contrast between judicial restraint and abdication of duty.

questions.question: Which constitutional basis for the directions is correctly stated in the passage?

options.A: The directions rest on Article 226, as the petition was filed before a High Court and transferred to the Supreme Court
options.B: The directions rest only on Article 14, since the Court found no violation of Article 21 in the continued detention
options.C: The directions rest on Article 72, because the Court exercised the power of clemency in respect of the elderly prisoners
options.D: The directions rest on Article 21 as the substantive source, with Articles 32 and 142 as the source of the Court's power to issue them, and the petition invoked Article 14 as well, in the context of prisoners who are aged or terminally ill

questions.explanation: The petition was under Articles 14 and 21, and the Court issued directions under Articles 32 and 142.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C confuses the Court's directions with executive clemency, which is exercised by the President under Article 72. Option B contradicts the passage. Option A invents a transfer from a High Court.
questions.clat_trap: Clemency, remission and release are related ideas, so Article 72 attracts a hasty reader.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The direction that independent Medical Boards certify terminal illness is meant to

options.A: transfer the power of premature release from the State governments to the medical profession
options.B: fix a single age above which every prisoner must be released without any further inquiry
options.C: replace the Under Trial Review Committees, abolished by the judgment
options.D: supply an objective and reviewable medical basis for release applications

questions.explanation: The Boards certify illness or vulnerability so that decisions are reasoned and subject to judicial review; they do not decide release.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A gives the medical boards a power the Court did not give. Option B invents automatic release by age. Option C reverses the passage, which retains the Review Committees.
questions.clat_trap: The passage describes both Boards and Committees, and the wrong options garble their roles.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A prisoner aged seventy-two, who is serving a life sentence and is in good health, relies on the judgment to claim release. On the passage, his claim

options.A: fails because the judgment applies only to undertrials and excludes convicted prisoners serving life sentences
options.B: succeeds automatically, because the judgment fixes seventy years as the age beyond which every convict must be released
options.C: fails to the extent that it rests on age alone, as the judgment requires a policy with a time-bound and reasoned process and does not mandate release by reason of age as such
options.D: succeeds only if the Medical Board certifies that he is terminally ill, since age is not a relevant factor under the judgment

questions.explanation: The Court directed States to frame a policy with a reasoned process; it did not command release by age alone, and its target group includes convicts and undertrials above seventy as well as the terminally ill.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B turns a policy direction into automatic release. Option D ignores that age above seventy is itself a category in the petition. Option A contradicts the passage, which covers convicts.
questions.clat_trap: The number seventy appears in the petition, and a student may confuse a category with a right to release.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The passage links the judgment to Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1978) because both

options.A: prescribe a uniform definition of terminal illness for all prisons in the country
options.B: hold that a prisoner has a fundamental right to be released on grounds of old age or illness
options.C: affirm that prisoners keep fundamental rights while in custody
options.D: recognise a power in the Court to grant remission of sentences in place of the Government

questions.explanation: Sunil Batra held that prisoners retain their fundamental rights, which is the idea in the Court's opening statement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B overstates the effect of both judgments. Option A attributes to Sunil Batra a definition that belongs to the 2026 directions. Option D invents a power of remission in the Court.
questions.clat_trap: The overstated options use 'fundamental right to be released', which is far wider than the cases.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Consider the following statements on the judgment. I. The Court directed the Centre, States and Union Territories to notify a policy within three months. II. The Court fixed a single age at which all prisoners must be released. III. Under Trial Review Committees are to review eligible prisoners periodically. IV. The directions were issued under Articles 32 and 142.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, III and IV only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I and IV only

questions.explanation: I, III and IV are stated in the passage. II is false because the Court directed a policy and did not fix an age for release.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Statement II treats a policy direction as an automatic entitlement.
questions.clat_trap: The statement about an age limit attracts those who remember the age of seventy from the petition.
questions.language_trick: 'must be released' is a stronger claim than 'frame a policy'.

passages.subject_area: Criminal Law (Sentencing and Remission) and Constitutional Law
passages.title: Proportionate Punishment and the Governor's Remission Power: Ehsaan and Parveen Kumar (2026)
passages.passage:
Two judgments of July 2026, both authored by Justice Sanjay Karol, show how the Supreme Court now speaks of the length of imprisonment. In Ehsaan v State (NCT of Delhi) (20 July 2026; Karol and Augustine George Masih JJ.), the appellant, then aged 25, had been convicted of gang rape under Section 376D of the Penal Code (now Section 70 of the BNS) for an offence of September 2016 and sentenced to imprisonment for the remainder of his natural life. The conviction was left undisturbed; only the sentence was examined. The Bench began: “When a sentence is imposed on an offender, it is done so with trifold purpose i.e. punitive, deterrent and protective.” It then listed factors, among them the age of the accused and “Consider the possibility of reformation of the accused”, adding “It is the duty of the State to establish that the same does not exist”, and cautioned that “The facets identified by us above are illustrative and not exhaustive.” The State had shown nothing against reformation, and the appellant, with no criminal antecedents, had kept good conduct for nearly ten years including remission. The Court held that “given the young age there is a possibility of reformation” and modified the sentence to 20 years with the benefit of remission, if any. It went no lower, reasoning that since the 2013 amendment the section prescribes twenty years as the minimum and the older power to impose less for adequate and special reasons has gone.
The doctrinal background matters. In Swamy Shraddananda (2008) the Court first devised fixed-term sentences beyond fourteen years but short of death; a Constitution Bench confirmed in Union of India v V. Sriharan (2015) that courts may do so; and Maru Ram v Union of India (1980) had held that the powers under Articles 72 and 161 operate independently of statutory remission under Sections 432-433A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
In Parveen Kumar @ Parveen Chauhan v State of Haryana (1 July 2026; Karol and N. Kotiswar Singh JJ.), a life convict (convicted in 2009), who had served over fourteen years, sought release under Haryana's 2002 remission policy. The State applied its 2008 policy, which required twenty years of actual and twenty-five years of total imprisonment. The Court held the 2002 policy to be an exercise under Article 161, as the three-judge Bench in State of Haryana v Jagdish (2010) had held of the earlier 1993 policy, so that a later policy framed under Sections 432 and 433 CrPC “cannot override an exercise of power under Article 161, for that power is distinct and independent”. State of Haryana v Raj Kumar (2021), a two-judge decision that had treated the 2002 policy as statutory, was declared per incuriam because it “would fall foul of the reasoning in Jagdish supra”. The State was directed to reconsider the application within four weeks; the ruling is prospective and does not reopen decided applications.
verbatim_extracts: When a sentence is imposed on an offender, it is done so with trifold purpose i.e. punitive, deterrent and protective.
Consider the possibility of reformation of the accused
It is the duty of the State to establish that the same does not exist
The facets identified by us above are illustrative and not exhaustive.
given the young age there is a possibility of reformation
cannot override an exercise of power under Article 161, for that power is distinct and independent
would fall foul of the reasoning in Jagdish supra

questions.question: On the passage, the Court in Ehsaan placed the burden of dealing with the possibility of the appellant's reformation on

options.A: the State, which must show by material on record that he cannot be reformed
options.B: the probation officer, whose report is a precondition to any reduction
options.C: the trial court, which must record a separate finding on reformation at the time of conviction
options.D: the convict, who must prove his reform through a sworn record of conduct kept in custody

questions.explanation: The Court listed possibility of reformation as a factor and added that it is the State's duty to establish that it does not exist. Since the State placed nothing on record, the plea stood unrebutted.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reverses the burden. Option C invents a finding the Court never required. Option B adds a procedural precondition that does not appear in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The burden of proof is moved to the person who gains from the plea in options that sound procedurally orthodox.
questions.language_trick: 'the same' in the quotation refers back to the possibility of reformation, so a quick reader may attach it to the factor above it.

questions.question: The Court in Ehsaan stopped at twenty years and did not reduce the sentence further because

options.A: fixed-term sentences under Swamy Shraddananda are open only where the Court is also considering the death penalty for the offence
options.B: the appellant had spent ten years in custody and the law requires at least fifteen before a court may interfere with a sentence
options.C: the State proved that the appellant had a criminal history which showed that reformation was no longer realistically possible
options.D: the present section fixes twenty years as the floor and no longer lets courts go lower

questions.explanation: After the 2013 amendment, twenty years is the minimum under the section and the earlier power to impose less for adequate and special reasons is gone. The Court therefore respected the legislative floor.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C contradicts the passage, which says the State showed nothing against reformation. Option A imports a limit on Swamy Shraddananda that the passage does not state. Option B invents a fifteen-year threshold.
questions.clat_trap: Several options mention periods and precedents that sound technical, which draws attention away from the plain statutory floor.
questions.language_trick: 'went no lower' signals a floor, not a ceiling.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best reading of the statement that the factors listed in Ehsaan 'are illustrative and not exhaustive'?

options.A: The list is a closed set, so a court may not look at any consideration outside it when it decides the quantum of punishment in a given case
options.B: A sentencing court may take into account other relevant circumstances also, apart from the factors the Bench listed
options.C: The list binds the trial court, while the High Court hearing a sentence appeal may ignore the factors
options.D: The list is a mandatory checklist, and omission of any factor makes the conviction unsustainable

questions.explanation: 'Illustrative' means examples are given; 'not exhaustive' means other considerations may also count.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats the list as exhaustive. Option C distinguishes trial and appellate courts without any basis. Option D turns a guide for sentencing into a ground for setting aside the conviction.
questions.clat_trap: Misreading 'illustrative' as 'mandatory' or 'exhaustive'.
questions.language_trick: 'illustrative and not exhaustive' is a double negative pair students invert under time pressure.

questions.question: State of Haryana v Raj Kumar (2021) was declared per incuriam in Parveen Kumar because

options.A: it treated the 2002 policy as statutory merely because no source of power was named, a view contrary to the reasoning of the larger Bench in Jagdish
options.B: it applied the 2008 policy retrospectively to a convict who had already served more than fourteen years of life imprisonment
options.C: it was decided by a Bench of two judges and so could not be followed in any circumstance by a later Bench of equal strength
options.D: it ignored Maru Ram, which had held that Sections 432 and 433 CrPC prevail over remission under Article 161

questions.explanation: The per incuriam finding rests on conflict with the three-judge decision in Jagdish, which had treated the earlier policy as an Article 161 exercise.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C relies on bench strength alone, which is not what makes a decision per incuriam. Option B describes a different fact of the case. Option D reverses Maru Ram, which protected Articles 72 and 161.
questions.clat_trap: 'Per incuriam' is often linked to smaller benches; the real test is overlooking binding law.
questions.language_trick: 'merely because no source of power was named' pinpoints the faulty step in Raj Kumar.

questions.question: A State issues, after the BNSS comes into force, a stricter remission policy under the BNSS provision that replaces Section 432 CrPC. A convict claims release under an earlier policy issued by the Governor under Article 161. On the reasoning in Parveen Kumar, the likely position is that

options.A: the later policy governs him, since statutory policies made later always displace earlier executive policies on the same subject
options.B: the earlier policy lapses on commencement of the BNSS, which repeals the CrPC provisions on remission
options.C: the earlier Article 161 policy continues to govern, because a statutory policy cannot override the constitutional power
options.D: the convict may rely on the earlier policy only if the Governor re-affirms it by a fresh personal order after the BNSS commences in the State

questions.explanation: The reasoning is that the Article 161 power is distinct and independent, so a policy under the ordinary statute cannot override it. The change of statute does not change that.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states a general rule the Court rejected for Article 161 policies. Option B confuses repeal of statutory provisions with the constitutional source. Option D invents a re-affirmation requirement.
questions.clat_trap: A new statute seems to wipe out earlier instruments; the answer depends on the constitutional, not statutory, source of the earlier policy.
questions.language_trick: 'after the BNSS comes into force' is a distractor; the source of power decides.

questions.question: Assertion (A): In Ehsaan the Court upheld the conviction but reduced a sentence of imprisonment for the remainder of natural life to twenty years. Reason (R): The Court held that a sentence below the statutory minimum is open to the Court whenever the State fails to disprove the possibility of reformation.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is true since the sentence was modified to twenty years with remission, if any. R is false: the Court did not go below the twenty-year minimum and reasoned that the power to go lower had been removed.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R states a power the Court expressly said does not exist.
questions.clat_trap: Students see the reformation reasoning and assume it justifies going below the floor.
questions.language_trick: 'whenever' overstates the Court's reasoning.

passages.title: Heinous Offences, Preliminary Assessment and Age at the Bail Stage: X v State of Bihar and Anurudh (2026)
passages.passage:
X v State of Bihar (22 July 2026; 2026 INSC 728; J.B. Pardiwala and Ujjal Bhuyan JJ.) concerned a boy, over sixteen at the time, accused of murder. The Juvenile Justice Board, by majority, held that he need not be tried as an adult; the appellate court reversed and the Patna High Court agreed. Under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 an offence is “heinous” (Section 2(33)) if the minimum punishment is seven years or more. Offences with no minimum, or a minimum below seven years but a maximum above seven, fall in the “serious” band (Section 2(54)), the so-called fourth category recognised in Shilpa Mittal v State (NCT of Delhi) (2020). Section 302 of the Penal Code prescribes “death, or imprisonment for life”, and the appellant argued that, since no minimum is written, murder could only be “serious”. The Court rejected the argument: “the word “or” merely confers upon the court the discretion to choose between the two punishments” and “it cannot be said that no minimum punishment exists”. Life imprisonment is treated as a minimum above seven years, so murder is heinous. Section 21, which bars a life sentence without possibility of release for a juvenile, operates at the stage of sentencing and does not alter classification, and Shilpa Mittal was distinguished.
The Court also gave guidelines on the preliminary assessment under Section 15. The Board “must not express any view, draw any inference” on guilt. It examines the child's mental and physical capacity, ability to understand the consequences and the circumstances of the offence. The expert report is one input; the Board must also consider the Social Background Report, Social Investigation Report and witness statements. Under Section 101(2), the appellate court has a discretion, not a duty, to seek expert help.
State of UP v Anurudh (9 January 2026; 2026 INSC 47; Sanjay Karol and N. Kotiswar Singh JJ.) arose from a bail order in a POCSO case in which the High Court had ordered medical tests on the victim's age and directed such tests in every POCSO investigation. The Supreme Court set this aside. Age is a matter for trial; Section 94 of the JJ Act gives the method (documents first, medical test only if documents are unavailable); and a bail court exercising Section 439 CrPC cannot hold a mini-trial. Noting misuse, it observed: “Misuse of the POCSO Act highlights a grim societal chasm – on the one end children are silenced by fear” (extract), and sent the judgment to the Union Law Secretary to consider a “Romeo-Juliet clause” for genuine adolescent relationships.
verbatim_extracts: the word “or” merely confers upon the court the discretion to choose between the two punishments
it cannot be said that no minimum punishment exists
must not express any view, draw any inference
Misuse of the POCSO Act highlights a grim societal chasm – on the one end children are silenced by fear

questions.question: On the passage, the appellant in X v State of Bihar contended that murder was only a 'serious' offence because

options.A: the Act classifies as heinous only offences carrying a minimum of ten years of imprisonment, which a life sentence does not clearly satisfy
options.B: Section 302 of the Penal Code says death or life imprisonment and prescribes no minimum, so no minimum exists
options.C: Section 21 of the Act bars life imprisonment for a juvenile, so murder by a child can only fall in the lesser band of offences
options.D: Shilpa Mittal had expressly held murder by a person above sixteen to be a serious offence under the Act

questions.explanation: The argument was textual: no minimum is written in Section 302, so the offence could not satisfy the minimum-seven-years test.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states a different threshold; the Act says seven years. Option C confuses a rule on sentencing with classification. Option D attributes to Shilpa Mittal a holding it does not have.
questions.clat_trap: The question asks what the appellant argued, not what the Court held; two options mix up the two.
questions.language_trick: 'contended' flags that the stated ground is a party's argument.

questions.question: The Court's reading of the word 'or' in 'death, or imprisonment for life' is that it

options.A: creates a presumption in favour of life imprisonment which the Board may rebut by an expert report
options.B: gives the court a discretion to choose between two punishments, without removing the minimum that applies
options.C: shows that Parliament left the minimum open, so the Board must fix it case by case
options.D: makes the two punishments equal alternatives so that a minimum cannot exist for any offence worded in this way, whatever the Act says

questions.explanation: The word confers a choice of punishments; it does not mean that there is no minimum.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D turns the choice into the absence of a floor. Option C hands a sentencing function to the Board. Option A invents a rebuttable presumption.
questions.clat_trap: Familiar rule of reading disjunctives is made to look decisive.
questions.language_trick: 'merely confers' limits the effect of 'or'.

questions.question: Shilpa Mittal did not help the appellant because

options.A: it dealt with offences having no minimum or a minimum below seven years, which does not describe an offence whose lower punishment is life imprisonment
options.B: it was overruled in the present case, since the Court held that a fourth category of offences cannot exist under the Act
options.C: it was decided before the Act of 2015 came into force and therefore has no bearing on the interpretation of its provisions
options.D: it dealt only with offences under special statutes, to which the Penal Code offence of murder cannot be compared for classification

questions.explanation: The 'fourth category' concerns offences with no minimum or a minimum below seven years; murder, whose lower punishment is life imprisonment, is outside it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D invents a restriction to special statutes. Option C is wrong on timing; Shilpa Mittal (2020) came after the Act. Option B says it was overruled, while the Court distinguished it.
questions.clat_trap: 'Distinguished' and 'overruled' are different, and options exploit the confusion.
questions.language_trick: 'does not describe' ties the case to the category, not to the label 'serious'.

questions.question: A Juvenile Justice Board, in its preliminary assessment, records that the child 'planned the offence and is therefore guilty', relying only on a psychologist's report. On the guidelines in the passage, the order is

options.A: open to challenge, as the Board must not infer guilt and must weigh the social background and investigation reports with the expert report
options.B: valid, because planning is a relevant circumstance of the offence, and guilt may be inferred from it for deciding on trial as an adult, as the Board thinks fit in each case
options.C: valid, because the expert report is conclusive on mental capacity and no other material needs to be considered
options.D: open to challenge only because the appellate court, and not the Board, is the authority to decide on trial as an adult

questions.explanation: The assessment is not an inquiry into guilt. The Board must consider all inputs, and the expert report is only one.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C makes the expert report conclusive. Option B allows an inference on guilt. Option D misplaces the authority; the Board conducts the assessment.
questions.clat_trap: 'Therefore guilty' is the hidden error in the Board's order.
questions.language_trick: 'only' in the last option narrows the ground wrongly.

questions.question: According to the passage, a medical test to determine the age of the victim in a POCSO case is

options.A: to be ordered by the bail court whenever the age shown in school records is inconsistent with the statements of the victim
options.B: to be ordered at the start of every investigation as a mandatory step, so that disputes on age do not arise at the bail stage
options.C: not to be ordered automatically, but is a fallback where documents under Section 94 are not available
options.D: to be ordered only by the High Court, which alone can decide the age of a victim before trial

questions.explanation: Documents come first; a medical test is resorted to only if they are unavailable or cannot be relied on, and the decision belongs to trial.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B is the High Court direction that was set aside. Option A lets the bail court conduct a mini-trial. Option D invents a High Court monopoly.
questions.clat_trap: The High Court's own direction is placed as an option.
questions.language_trick: 'fallback' signals the secondary position of the medical test.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct on the passage?
I. Murder under Section 302 of the Penal Code is a heinous offence under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015.
II. In X v State of Bihar the Court held that the Board may express a prima facie view on guilt at the preliminary assessment.
III. In Anurudh the Court held that a bail court cannot conduct a mini-trial on the victim's age.
IV. In Anurudh the Court itself enacted a Romeo-Juliet exemption in the POCSO Act.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and III restate the passage. II is wrong because the Board must not draw an inference on guilt. IV is wrong because the Court only sent the judgment to the Law Secretary to consider such a clause.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: II reverses a guideline; IV turns a suggestion into legislation.
questions.clat_trap: 'Suggestion' versus 'enactment': courts cannot legislate.
questions.language_trick: 'itself enacted' is the error word in IV.

passages.subject_area: Judicial Process, Technology and Constitutional Law
passages.title: Hallucinated Precedents and Court Recordings: Pooja Ramesh Singh and Harshita Grover (2026)
passages.passage:
Two orders of July 2026 show the Supreme Court responding to technology inside the court. In Pooja Ramesh Singh v Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd. (2 July 2026; 2026 SCC OnLine SC 1258; P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe JJ.), the Bank invoked a corporate guarantee and filed an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The NCLT, Mumbai admitted it on 28 August 2024, and the NCLAT's order of 11 September 2025 followed. The Supreme Court found that both bodies had relied on non-existent, fake and hallucinated precedents, allegedly generated through artificial intelligence. It said: “This is yet again a case where the Tribunal relied on non-existent, fake and hallucinated material”, and on the legal effect: “A decision of a Court or an adjudicating authority based on material which is fake and hallucinated is no decision at all”. Noting that “Today's courts and tribunals implicitly trust lawyers when referring to precedents cited before them”, the Court set aside both orders, restored the Section 7 application for fresh decision (preferably within two weeks), kept the parties on status quo, expressed no view on the merits, and asked the Bar Council of India to constitute a committee to frame principles and disciplinary consequences. It spoke of zero tolerance but accepted that AI may be an aid under human control.
In Harshita Grover v Union of India (24 July 2026; CJI Surya Kant, Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana JJ.), the concern was the circulation of cropped, out-of-context clips of live-streamed hearings. Live-streaming rests on Swapnil Tripathi v Supreme Court of India (2018), where the Court accepted that open justice under Article 21 can be advanced by broadcasting proceedings, and Model Rules later followed. By an interim order the Court barred the extraction, posting, monetisation and hosting of audio-video recordings of proceedings on social media and digital platforms without prior permission of the Secretary General of the Supreme Court or the Registrar General of the High Court concerned. The High Courts and platforms such as YouTube, X, Meta, Google and LinkedIn were impleaded, and the High Courts were asked to report on the feasibility of continuous live-streaming. The Court clarified that the order “shall have no bearing on the reporting of court proceedings by recognised news outlets”. (Later clarifications about news outlets' use of clips: verify current status.)
verbatim_extracts: This is yet again a case where the Tribunal relied on non-existent, fake and hallucinated material
A decision of a Court or an adjudicating authority based on material which is fake and hallucinated is no decision at all
Today's courts and tribunals implicitly trust lawyers when referring to precedents cited before them
shall have no bearing on the reporting of court proceedings by recognised news outlets

questions.question: The Supreme Court's holding in Pooja Ramesh Singh is that a decision resting on fake AI-generated precedents

options.A: is only an irregularity which can be cured by imposing costs on the advocate who cited it
options.B: may be saved by the appellate body substituting genuine precedents without hearing the parties again on the issue
options.C: stands unless the affected party proves that the fake precedent changed the outcome on merits and so caused prejudice
options.D: is no decision at all in the eyes of law, so the matter has to be decided afresh on genuine precedents

questions.explanation: The Court said such a decision is 'no decision at all' and restored the application for fresh adjudication.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C imports a prejudice requirement. Option B allows silent substitution of precedents. Option A reduces the defect to an irregularity.
questions.clat_trap: Tempting to treat it as a curable irregularity as in many procedural defects.
questions.language_trick: 'no decision at all' is stronger than 'wrong decision'.

questions.question: Which of the following did the Court NOT do in Pooja Ramesh Singh?

options.A: Imposed a ban on use of artificial intelligence by advocates for drafting
options.B: Restored the Section 7 application to the file of the NCLT for expeditious decision without expressing any view on the merits
options.C: Asked the Bar Council of India to constitute a committee to frame guiding principles and disciplinary consequences for such reliance
options.D: Set aside the orders of both the NCLT and the NCLAT and directed the parties to maintain status quo until disposal

questions.explanation: The Court accepted that AI may be used as an aid under human control. It did not ban it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C, Option B and Option D are all things the Court did.
questions.clat_trap: A NOT stem: three options are true statements of the order.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT' reverses the usual pattern; the plausible-sounding 'ban' is the false one.

questions.question: The significance of Swapnil Tripathi (2018) for the later order in Harshita Grover is that

options.A: it held that broadcasting proceedings is a fundamental right of the press that is enforceable against every Registrar General
options.B: it accepted live-streaming as part of open justice under Article 21, so the later order restricts downstream use of recordings and does not stop live-streaming itself
options.C: it left the use of recordings entirely to the platforms, which the later order now withdraws by a general direction
options.D: it prohibited live-streaming in principle, so the later order simply repeats that prohibition for social media platforms alone

questions.explanation: The 2018 decision supports broadcasting as a part of open justice; the interim order deals with extraction and monetisation of recordings.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reverses the 2018 position. Option C invents a delegation to platforms. Option A converts open justice into a press right.
questions.clat_trap: A restriction on circulation looks like a reversal of live-streaming.
questions.language_trick: 'does not stop live-streaming itself' is the key limit.

questions.question: A newspaper publishes a text report of a hearing in the Supreme Court. A YouTuber posts a cropped clip of the live-stream with a caption and earns advertising revenue. On the interim order as described in the passage,

options.A: the clip is permitted if it is accurate, but monetisation alone needs the permission of the Registrar General concerned
options.B: the text report is outside the order, while the clip needs prior permission and its monetisation is barred
options.C: both the report and the clip are barred, since the order stops every form of public dissemination
options.D: both are permitted, since the order applies only to unrecognised news outlets and not to individual content creators

questions.explanation: The order has no bearing on reporting; it bars extraction, posting and monetisation of recordings without permission.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C extends the bar to reports. Option D inverts the exception. Option A adds an accuracy defence the order does not state.
questions.clat_trap: The exception for 'recognised news outlets' invites a wrong inference about who is covered.
questions.language_trick: 'reporting' versus 'recordings': two different things.

questions.question: In Pooja Ramesh Singh the Bar Council of India was asked to

options.A: constitute a committee to frame principles and prescribe disciplinary consequences for relying on or submitting fake material as precedent
options.B: suspend the practice licence of advocates who appeared for the parties before the NCLT and the NCLAT in the matter
options.C: certify every AI research tool before an advocate may use it for legal work in any court or tribunal in India
options.D: frame rules making every citation of an unreported case by an advocate an offence under the Advocates Act, without any further inquiry into the advocate's intent or knowledge

questions.explanation: The Court asked for a committee on guiding principles and disciplinary consequences.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D creates a blanket offence. Option C creates a certification regime. Option B imposes a sanction on named advocates without inquiry.
questions.clat_trap: The correct option is institutional and the wrong options are punitive.
questions.language_trick: 'constitute a committee' versus 'frame rules'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): In Pooja Ramesh Singh the Supreme Court decided the merits of the Section 7 IBC application. Reason (R): The Court set aside the orders of the NCLT and the NCLAT because they relied on fake precedents.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false: the Court expressed no view on merits and restored the application for fresh decision. R is true as the orders were set aside for reliance on fake material.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R's truth and A's falsity are both inferable from the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A fresh-adjudication remand looks like a decision on the case.
questions.language_trick: 'decided the merits' is contradicted by 'expressed no view'.

passages.title: Student Data and the Right to Refuse: Abhishek Baxi v Union of India (2026)
passages.passage:
Abhishek Baxi v Union of India (Writ Petition (Civil) 832 of 2026; order of 20 July 2026; CJI Surya Kant, Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana JJ.) tested APAAR, the Automated Permanent Academic Account Registry, a Ministry of Education scheme introduced in July 2023 that gives each student a unique lifelong ID, linked to Aadhaar, to hold academic records. The scheme is described as voluntary, but the parents of four students argued that examinations and records effectively required the ID, that the fixed consent form allowed no informed refusal or revocation, and that the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act), including its provision on consent, was not being followed. Counsel relied on the Aadhaar judgment (2018), for the proposition that children cannot be compelled to obtain Aadhaar, and on the nine-judge decision in Puttaswamy (2017) recognising privacy as a fundamental right.
The Court did not strike the scheme down. The CJI observed from the bench: “Let us not doubt everything in the country with a suspicious eye; it is a welcome step.” But it adopted, nationwide, paragraph 19 of the Orissa High Court's decision in Rohit Anand Das v State of Odisha (December 2025), which had held that withdrawing consent later cannot replace the right to refuse at the outset, so that the consent form must let parents decline. The order records that “such a safeguard is essential to ensure that the requirement of consent is meaningful and informed”; that APAAR data processing “shall, therefore, be strictly governed by the provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023”; and that the administrative nature of the scheme “does not absolve the authorities of their obligations in relation to the protection of personal data”. Personal information “cannot be disclosed, shared, or otherwise made available to any private entity or third party” except as permitted by law and for authorised purposes of the scheme. The Court gave no specific direction on Aadhaar and disposed of the petition with liberty to the respondents to seek clarification, as they had not been heard.
verbatim_extracts: Let us not doubt everything in the country with a suspicious eye; it is a welcome step.
such a safeguard is essential to ensure that the requirement of consent is meaningful and informed
shall, therefore, be strictly governed by the provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
does not absolve the authorities of their obligations in relation to the protection of personal data
cannot be disclosed, shared, or otherwise made available to any private entity or third party

questions.question: The Court's response to the challenge to APAAR was to

options.A: allow the scheme to continue, require a nationwide consent form that lets parents decline, and subject data processing to the DPDP Act
options.B: strike the scheme down as unconstitutional, because it links a student's academic record to Aadhaar without any statutory basis or safeguards for the child's data
options.C: direct that the scheme be made mandatory for all students, so as to avoid selective enrolment and uneven records
options.D: uphold the scheme in full, leaving the question of consent to be decided by the schools according to their own policies

questions.explanation: The Court neither struck down nor endorsed the scheme unconditionally; it adopted safeguards on consent and data.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B claims invalidation. Option D omits the safeguards. Option C invents a mandate.
questions.clat_trap: Two options pick extreme outcomes; the Court chose a conditional middle.
questions.language_trick: 'continue' and 'require' together signal a conditional order.

questions.question: The Court adopted the approach of the Orissa High Court because

options.A: consent forms for educational schemes are void if they do not contain a separate clause on Aadhaar linkage as required by law in every State
options.B: withdrawal of consent afterwards is no substitute for refusing at the start, and consent must be meaningful and informed
options.C: the Orissa decision had been affirmed by the Supreme Court earlier and was therefore binding on all authorities
options.D: a parent who has once given consent loses the right to withdraw it later, so refusal at the very outset must be allowed by the school

questions.explanation: The passage says withdrawing consent later cannot replace the right to refuse at the outset.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D reverses the logic about withdrawal. Option C invents an earlier affirmation. Option A invents a legal rule on consent forms.
questions.clat_trap: The Orissa decision is a High Court ruling, so a binding-precedent argument is tempting but false.
questions.language_trick: 'meaningful and informed' sets the standard for consent.

questions.question: The statement that the scheme's administrative nature 'does not absolve the authorities of their obligations in relation to the protection of personal data' means that

options.A: the DPDP Act applies only to the schemes which are enacted by Parliament and not to those that are administered by executive instructions
options.B: the administrative character of the scheme makes the authorities liable to criminal prosecution for any breach of the data rules
options.C: a scheme run by executive instructions is still bound by the data protection statute, so authorities cannot claim exemption merely because it is administrative
options.D: authorities are exempt from the Act if the data is held for an academic purpose and not for any commercial use

questions.explanation: The point is that the absence of a statute behind the scheme does not remove the duties imposed by the DPDP Act.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the meaning. Option D imports an academic-purpose exemption. Option B jumps to criminal liability.
questions.clat_trap: 'Absolve' is the key verb; the wrong options reverse or exaggerate its effect.
questions.language_trick: 'does not absolve' is a negative that students read as 'absolves'.

questions.question: An education board proposes to share APAAR records with a private ed-tech company which offers coaching, citing improved 'student outcomes'. On the order as described, the proposal is
