options.A: impermissible only if the company is a foreign entity, since the order concerns cross-border sharing of student data
options.B: permissible, if parents were given an opt-out form at enrolment and did not use the option to refuse consent
options.C: impermissible, since the order bars disclosure to a private entity beyond the authorised purposes of the scheme, whatever benefit is claimed for students
options.D: permissible, if the company signs an undertaking that the data will be used only for improving academic outcomes

questions.explanation: The order bars sharing with private entities or third parties except as permitted by law and for authorised scheme purposes.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats silence as consent for a new purpose. Option D relies on an undertaking, which the order does not mention. Option A limits the bar to foreign entities.
questions.clat_trap: A beneficial purpose looks like an authorised purpose.
questions.language_trick: 'beyond the scope of the Scheme' defines the limit.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT stated in the order, as reproduced in the passage?

options.A: A direction that personal information not be shared with a private entity or third party except as permitted by law
options.B: A direction striking down the Aadhaar-linked registration requirement as violative of the right to privacy
options.C: Liberty to the respondents to seek clarification, since they had not been heard at the stage of the order
options.D: A direction that processing of APAAR data be governed by the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

questions.explanation: The order gave no specific direction on Aadhaar and did not strike down the requirement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D, Option A and Option C are stated in the order.
questions.clat_trap: A NOT stem; the plausible-sounding but absent direction is the answer.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT stated' invites choosing the first true-sounding option.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct on the passage?
I. The Court directed that the consent form allow parents to refuse consent.
II. The Court declared APAAR unconstitutional insofar as it requires Aadhaar linkage.
III. APAAR data processing is to be governed by the DPDP Act, 2023.
IV. The respondents were given liberty to seek clarification because they had not been heard.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, III and IV only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I and IV only

questions.explanation: I, III and IV restate the passage. II is wrong; the Court gave no specific direction on Aadhaar.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: II is the odd one out and is dressed as a natural consequence of the case.
questions.clat_trap: A challenge on Aadhaar does not mean that the Court decided Aadhaar.
questions.language_trick: 'declared ... unconstitutional' is the unsupported claim.

passages.title: Daughters, Marriage and Compassionate Appointment: Sayara Khatoon v State of Bihar (2026)
passages.passage:
Sayara Khatoon @ Shajara Khatoon v State of Bihar (order of 23 July 2026; 2026 LiveLaw (SC) 745; M.M. Sundresh and Prasanna B. Varale JJ.) arose from the death of a government employee. His daughter's request for compassionate appointment was rejected, partly because of an objection by her maternal uncle (later removed by a no-objection certificate) and partly because Bihar's policy of 10 December 2014 made only divorced or deserted daughters eligible. She said that her divorce was not formally recognised, that she lived with her parental family and that her mother and brother supported her. The State argued that the policy was not under challenge, that compassionate appointment is a matter of policy and not a right, and that a daughter ordinarily leaves her parental home on marriage. The Patna High Court upheld the rejection.
The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and the rejection and struck down the policy's condition. It held: “This Court has repeatedly held that any classification differentiating a daughter from a son is, per se, unconstitutional.” The restriction of eligibility to divorced or deserted daughters “cannot be sustained in the eye of law”. The Court rejected the State's premise: “There cannot be a presumption in law that, after marriage, a daughter severs her ties with her parental family and resides with husband in her matrimonial home.” And it added: “In any event, adopting a hyper-technical approach cannot be a ground to deny consideration of her claim for compassionate appointment.” The State must consider her claim on merits within eight weeks.
The history is relevant. In Umesh Kumar Nagpal v State of Haryana (1994) the Court described compassionate appointment as an exception to the general rule of equal opportunity in public employment under Articles 14 and 16, meant to relieve sudden financial distress and not a vested right. Article 16(2) bars discrimination in employment on grounds of sex, and decisions such as Anuj Garg v Hotel Association of India (2008) and Joseph Shine v Union of India (2018) warned against laws founded on stereotypes about the roles of women. The 2026 order shows that even a scheme which is an exception to equality cannot rest on such a stereotype.
verbatim_extracts: This Court has repeatedly held that any classification differentiating a daughter from a son is, per se, unconstitutional.
cannot be sustained in the eye of law
There cannot be a presumption in law that, after marriage, a daughter severs her ties with her parental family and resides with husband in her matrimonial home.
In any event, adopting a hyper-technical approach cannot be a ground to deny consideration of her claim for compassionate appointment.

questions.question: In Sayara Khatoon the Supreme Court struck down

options.A: the restriction of eligibility, among daughters, to those who are divorced or deserted, since a classification differentiating a daughter from a son is per se unconstitutional
options.B: the rejection order only, leaving the condition on divorced and deserted daughters untouched for future applicants
options.C: the principle of compassionate appointment itself, which the Court held to be inconsistent with equal opportunity in public employment
options.D: the Bihar policy of December 2014 in its entirety, so that no dependant of a deceased employee can now claim appointment under it

questions.explanation: The Court struck down the condition restricting eligibility to divorced or deserted daughters and set aside the rejection.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D overstates the invalidation. Option C attacks the concept. Option B says that the condition survives.
questions.clat_trap: The remedy is narrow: a condition in a policy, not the policy or the concept.
questions.language_trick: 'the restriction of eligibility' is specific; 'in its entirety' is sweeping.

questions.question: The State's argument that a daughter ordinarily leaves her parental home on marriage fails because

options.A: the policy had not been challenged in the High Court, so the State could not defend it before the Supreme Court
options.B: the daughter in this case could show that her divorce had been formally recognised by a competent family court
options.C: the State has no power to make a policy on compassionate appointment, a matter for the legislature alone under Article 16
options.D: there is no presumption in law that marriage severs a daughter's ties with her family, and a public policy cannot be built on such a stereotype about daughters

questions.explanation: The Court said there cannot be a presumption in law that after marriage a daughter severs her ties with her parental family.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option C invents a legislative-only rule. Option B contradicts the facts, since her divorce was not formally recognised. Option A reverses the State's own argument.
questions.clat_trap: The facts are used as distractors; the reasoning concerns presumptions.
questions.language_trick: 'presumption in law' is the pivotal phrase.

questions.question: Which statement about Umesh Kumar Nagpal, as used in the passage, is accurate?

options.A: It held that distinctions between sons and daughters in compassionate appointment are valid if rational
options.B: It called compassionate appointment an exception to equality in public employment, meant to relieve sudden distress and not a right
options.C: It held that compassionate appointment is the general rule in public employment, subject only to an exception for open competition and merit
options.D: It held that compassionate appointment is a fundamental right of every dependant of a deceased government employee under Article 21 of the Constitution

questions.explanation: The 1994 decision treated it as an exception to Articles 14 and 16, not as a right.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option D converts the exception into a right. Option C reverses rule and exception. Option A attributes a view on sons and daughters that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: The case is easily remembered for 'no vested right' but options reverse the rule-exception relation.
questions.language_trick: 'exception' versus 'general rule'.

questions.question: A State policy gives compassionate appointment to the sons, and unmarried daughters, of a deceased employee but not to married daughters, though it includes a married son. On the reasoning in Sayara Khatoon, the policy is

options.A: constitutional, because unmarried daughters are covered and so no daughter is excluded on the ground of sex alone
options.B: constitutional, because compassionate appointment is a matter of policy and not of right, and courts must not interfere with the policy choices of the executive in such matters
options.C: unconstitutional only if the married daughter proves that her husband is unemployed and that she has no source of income
options.D: likely unconstitutional, as it differentiates daughters from sons on the basis of marriage, which the Court held to be per se unconstitutional

questions.explanation: A policy that treats a married daughter differently from a married son differentiates a daughter from a son, which the Court has held to be per se unconstitutional.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B relies on the argument the State made and lost. Option A ignores that a married son is eligible. Option C adds a means test that has no basis in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Partial coverage of daughters looks like absence of sex discrimination.
questions.language_trick: 'though it includes a married son' fixes the comparator.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the limit of the decision in Sayara Khatoon?

options.A: It requires the State to consider her claim on merits, not to appoint her
options.B: It makes compassionate appointment a fundamental right of every married daughter of a deceased government employee throughout the country
options.C: It directs the State to appoint her within eight weeks, since the High Court had already found that she was eligible
options.D: It holds that the 2014 policy is void as a whole, so that no divorced or deserted daughter may now be appointed under it

questions.explanation: The direction is to consider the claim on merits within eight weeks. The High Court had upheld the rejection.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B creates a new right. Option D says the whole policy fell. Option C misstates both the direction and the High Court's view.
questions.clat_trap: A remedy of 'consider' is mistaken for 'appoint'.
questions.language_trick: 'consider' is a procedural direction.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Compassionate appointment cannot be claimed as a vested right, yet in Sayara Khatoon the Court directed the State to consider the appellant's claim. Reason (R): A policy confining eligibility to divorced or deserted daughters was held to be unsustainable in law.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are accurate. The reason explains why the policy ground for refusal fell, but A rests on the distinction between a right to be considered and a right to be appointed; R does not explain that.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R explains the removal of the ground for rejection, not the distinction in A.
questions.clat_trap: Because both statements are about the same case, the link looks causal.
questions.language_trick: 'yet' in A signals a contrast that R does not resolve.
